subtopic: COMMITTEE TO REPORT ON MEMORIALS TO BE ERECTED ON BATTLEFIELDS TO COMMEMORATE HEROISM OF CANADIANS.

speakeroldname: Hon. HLTGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Militia and Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: COMMITTEE TO REPORT ON MEMORIALS TO BE ERECTED ON BATTLEFIELDS TO COMMEMORATE HEROISM OF CANADIANS.
speechtext:
I beg to move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by Hon. Mr. Crothers:
_ That a special committee be appointed to consider and report upon the question of what memorials, if any, should he erected on the battlefields of the late war to commemorate the gallantry of the Canadian troops and all matters arising out of or connected with the same, and that Messrs. Mewburn, Clark (Red Deer), Le-mieux, Bfiland, McCurdy, Peck, Mowat, Power

and Blake be the members of such committee, with power to sit during the sessions of the House.
He said: As the House is no doubt aware, during the past year, eight sites have been selected in France and Flanders for the purpose of erecting memorials to commemorate the victories of Canadian soldiers during the Great War. These sites which have be.en selected are in respect of the battles which are now known, and which will be known to history, under the following names:
1.	St. Julien, a battle which was fought during the month of April, 1915, and also known as the second battle of Ypres.
2.	The battle of Passehendaele, -a battle which extended from the 22nd October to the 17th November, 1917.
3.	The battle of Observatory Ridge, sometime known as the battle of St. Eloi, which extended from May until June in the year 1916.
4.	The battle of Viiny Ridge which took place on the 9th April, 1917, and continued till May 3 following.
5.	The battle of Arras which took place during the months of August and September. 1918.
6.	The battle of Bourlon Wood which took place on September 27, 1918.
7.	The battle of Courcelette, which was part of the great battle of the Somme, fought during the months of September and October, 1916.
8.	The battle of Amiens which took place during the months of August and September, 1918.
These eight sites have been acquired partly by purchase and partly by contributions from the Governments of France and Belgium. One site in particular has been contributed iby a private gentleman in France, Count de Francqville. As the House is aware $500,000 was placed in the Estimates last year for the purpose of erecting memorials. I think the only part of this money expended has been a payment of about $1,500 which was the net cost to Canada of acquiring these sites. All of these sites have now been conveyed to the Government of Canada. As the House is aware, in the Estimates of this year the only sum mentioned for this purpose is $10,000. That is to carry on the necessary work of survey, road construction, and the like. The Government deems it proper to ask the House to take the ^whole question into consideration, and for this purpose that a special committee of nine members be now appointed who will go fully into the facts and determine upon some general policy for the

erection of permanent memorials. It is for the appointment of such a committee that the motion is now made.

subtopic: MOTION TO TAKE MONDAYS FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS STANDS.
speechtext: The desire of the Government to advance business at this stage of the session may be right and proper, but I would like to point out that a material part of the Government's policy-to wit, the Budget-has not yet been brought down. I think it is a little unusual, in advance of the Budget, for the Government to take possession of days which are at the disposal of private members, and therefore I would ask my right hon. friend to give consideration to that fact before he presses this motion.

subtopic: MOTION TO TAKE MONDAYS FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS STANDS.
speechtext:
It is true, as my hon. friend says, that the Budget, which is usually and rightfully considered to be a very important part of the business of the session, is not yet down. But it is also true that there is abundance of Government business, in the shape of legislation and main Estimates, already before the House. Some Bills of importance have been advanced quite a considerable way towards completion, but yet have some progress, more or less difficult to make before they come to a conclusion. In other words there is before the House at present a sufficiency of Government business to employ its full time. It is for the House to consider, in a way, how long it wishes to remain in session. I have taken it as the general expression of opinion, that members on both sides are not anxious to stay here to transact business any longer than is necessary, and that therefore they would be in the mind to get along as quickly as possible with the Government programme. Since the beginning of the session we have had the usual private members' days, and one of them still remains open. It is apparent, I think, to those who have attended the daily sittings that private members have had, in the first place, an opportunity to dispose of, and have disposed of, a number of their most important motions. They have also had abundant opportunity to take up and dispose of motions which still remain upon the Order Paper. Those motions have been called time after time, and session after session, and many of them have been passed. That goes rather to prove that what remains of private members' business, in the way of resolutions, is not considered to be very pressing or very urgent. Therefore it now becomes time for us to consider the period at which we shall bring this session to a close, and what steps are necessary in order to bring about that desirable end. I am not anxious to press this

motion at the present time if my hon. friend feels that there is any necessity-
, although he has not quite shown any- for further delay. His objection has been that the Budget is not yet down. As to the Budget, what will be discussed in connection with it, it has not very much to do with a great deal of the legislation-with almost all of the legislation, in fact-that is ready for the House, and it does not have a great deal to do with a large number of the Estimates-which we may call routine or necessary estimate-whether we have a Budget or not, and which, Estimates notwithstanding the kind of Budget we may have, must yet be put through for the general purposes and services of the country. That is why I make the proposition that we should get down to the real business of the session and dispose of it as quickly as we can, decently and in order. However, I am quite willing to let the motion lie till another occasion, and bring it up again, in a day or two, this being a sort of advertisement of the intention and desire of the Government.

That the Governor In Council may appoint a secretary to the Purchasing Board, and may upon the recommendation of the board and with the consent of the Civil Service Commission, transfer to the board any members of the staff of the War Purchasing Commission at such sal-' aries as the Governor in Council shall appoint, but not exceeding the respective salaries which they are then receiving; and that such other officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the board may be appointed or transferred from any other portion of the public service under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, 1918, and that provision be made for the payment of the salary or increase of salary of any such officer, clerk or employee so transferred.
5.	That the board shall not, without the approval of the Governor in Council, purchase or agree to purchase any supplies except such as are included in estimates or requisitions sent to the board by the various portions of the public service.
6.	That as far as possible tenders shall be called for in respect of all purchases or contracts to be made by or under the authority of the board, and purchases shall be made from and contracts given to the lowest tenderer. If in any case tenders are not called for, or a purchase or contract is not made from or with the lowest tenderer, the reason therefor shall be clearly and fully recorded.

As the committee will remember, a purchasing commis-94

In view of the regularity and uniformity thus secured in the purchasing of supplies, of the wide distribution of forms of tenders and calls for supplies, and of the general saving made, the Government in 1918 extended by Order in Council the powers of the commission from the purchasing of war materials only to the purchasing of all supplies needed for "the Government service. From 1918, the commission carried on its operations on that more extended plane. The commission had power to enter into contracts and to purchase supplies, the matter of requisitioning being left entirely with the departments. The responsibility in that matter rested, of course, where it should rest; a department knew what supplies it wanted, their nature, quality and quantity, and the requisition in every case had to he made by the department interested. Th§ -commission, being a temporary purchasing commission, has from 1915 to the present time, rather taken the line of supervising and controlling the contracts than furnishing a machinery, in itself concentrated, for the whole purpose of administering, so to speak, the matters of tenders and contract for and inspection of supplies. Therefore, the different officers, or staffs in cases where a purchasing department was in existence before, have been carried on under the commission up to the present time, the work of the commission being in supervising the letting of contracts, in better specification and wider dissemmination of knowledge of what was wanted, in keeping records of calls for tenders, and in coordinating ail these matters so as to prevent- duplication and tend totvards general efficiency.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is it the intention to place all departments of Government under this purchasing commission? For instance, will the ' commission purchase for the Canadian National railways?
No, not for the railways; they are exempted.
How many purchasing agents are there in all the departments, and if this Bill passes, will the services of those purchasing agents be dispensed with?

I cannot tell my hon. friend the exact number of what are fully constituted purchasing agencies in the departments. Some departments have a well-constituted agency for purchasing; others purchase through different officers and members of their staffs; but with reference to all these, during the five years that the purchasing commission has been in operation until the present time, it has not been the policy of the commission to dispense with the services of officers who are engaged in purchasing for the. different departments. The commission has utilized the services of those officers who are efficient, and I think they have generally been found to be efficient, and has added such other officers as are necessary for the proper carrying on of its work. It is proposed that the purchasing board to be appointed under this Bill shall utilize the services of all efficient purchasing agents in the different departments. It is not the idea that these men shall be cast aside and a new set brought in. Gradually it will happen, as the experience of the purchasing commission has shown that with this concentration of effort there will be greater efficiency, and, compared with the volume of business, probably fewer officers will be required, but the natural increase of business that takes place will probably offset that. Therefore, there is no violent disruption intended of officers who are now doing good work under

the commission or in the different departments, and their services will continue to be utilized.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why is an exception made in the case of purchasing supplies for the railways? What argument can be urged in favour of exempting the railways that cannot be urged with regard to any other department of the Government?

I think a little thought with reference to the supplies which are required by railways will show my hon. friend' that it would not be advantageous but, on the contrary, very burdensome to have a central purchasing board which is buying supplies for the different departments undertake also the purchasing of supplies for the railways. The purchasing of supplies for departments of the Government is a very large business. The commission, with its less extensive field, though, of course, we have had extraordinary times, has in less than five years made contracts and purchases to the amount of over $250,000,000-more than a quarter of a billion of dollars. Last year the departments themselves, over and above the time and supply contracts which were made by the, commission, made purchases amounting to $48,000,000. Some departments were purchasers along fourteen different linesr and therefore were employing fourteen different sets of energy, and were making fourteen different kinds of competition in the goods that were needed. It is not considered advisable, at the present time at all events-I am not going to say that it never will be advisable-to include in the purchasing board's activities the purchasing of supplies for the railways. Of course, the supplies for the Department of Railways itself will be bought by the board, just the same as the supplies for any other department.
That is stationery only.
There might be a few other articles. You need a chair to sit down on sometimes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What about
the supplies for the merchant marine? Would they be purchased by the board?

Those things
which are necessary for the operation of the merchant marine will be bought by the company which runs that branch of the transportation department.
94i

The company is the
Government. There is something to be said in favour of the concentration of purchasing power in one quarter. Good business reasons can be given for that, but why cannot the same purpose be accomplished by assigning the whole business to some particular department with its ordinary employees, of whom we have a pretty numerous body now, and, according to some hon. members, a too numerous body? Why do you create another commission for this purpose? I can see an advantage in having a concentration of purchasing power in one quarter, but I am not so clear that it is necessary to create another commission. The tendency of these commissions is to get a bit away from responsible government. Sometimes a member of the Government acts as a connecting link, but the general tendency of these commissions is to separate themselves from government authority, and, consequently, in some degree from parliamentary authority. I think the Government could accomplish all the merit that is in their purpose by simply assigning this purchasing work to some one of the departments. We have a pretty numerous body of ministers now, and if there is any argument, and I think there is, in favour of the concentration of purchasing power my hon. friend has abandoned his whole argument ' when he does not apply it to the most important spending department of the Government for the railways will be the biggest purchasing department of the Government. My hon. friend is not going to camouflage the business by talking of purchases being made by the company. The company is the Government, and every argument my hon. friend has advanced in support o? this measure would be stronger if it included the purchase of supplies for the railways. As it is, we are going to allow the Minister of Railways to buy a chair, and possibly some stationery, but as respects the real work of the department that is not going to come under this at all. I think my hon. friend has not logically carried out his own argument. He has failed to apply his argument to the largest fields of governmental expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Acting

I do not think of any other at present.

What about

speechtext: What about the purchase of stock for the Department of Agriculture?

I shall have to make inquiries about that, but my impression at the moment is that the purchase of stock for stock-raising purposes by the Department of Agriculture would not be made by this board. With reference to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding)
I quite see that he agrees with the principle of a central purchasing power, and believes that it can accomplish much good. But his main contention is that it does not go far enough and that it should apply itself to the whole of the railway system which, by the new arrangements, will come under a common management. If my hon. friend will think for a moment he will understand that, taking into consideration the immensity of the purchases, their wide scope and their technical character in a great many respects, there will be a purchasing department in that railway system, well organized, and thoroughly effective. It will be an immense system, and I think sufficient work will be found for an independent purchasing commission organized for the railway itself. If my hon. friend takes any great railway corporation ' he will find that such is the system they adopt. The Canadian Pacific has one of the best equipped and most efficient purchasing systems in the world, and all the great railway and business organizations to-day have this distinct feature that their purchases are not made by haphazard or in detail. Their purchases are made under a systematized co-operative uniform management w'here there is one directive energy behind the policy which guides the operation from the top to the bottom and which applies its directive power to all lines of purchasing down to the smallest detail. It would to my mind unnecessarily burden the system, and I do not think it would be advantageous in the result in the main that all the departments of the public service and of the vast railway system with its correlated marine service should be placed under this proposed management.
fSir George Foster.]

My right hon. friend was unfortunate in his reference to the Canadian Pacific. If the Canadian Pacific were to adopt the excellent system which he describes and then, having resolved to do that, were to say that as respects seventy-five per cent of the purchases the system shall not apply at all, that wodld be a fair parallel, because that is what the Government are doing. They are adopting a sound principle-I am rather in sympathy with it -but they immediately decide that as respects our greatest purchasing department this method shall not come into operation at all. The right hon. gentleman speaks of an independent purchasing commission for the railways. He is giving us a semblance of responsible government in this resolution for he is providing that the chairman of the board shall be a minister of the Crown. That is the link by which we keep it in contact with Parliament, but as respects all these railway purchases we are to have no power at all. There is to be an independent board with absolutely no parliamentary control. My right hon. friend starts in to reform the purchasing system and he winds up with a resolution: Resolved that this is a good system but as respects fifty or seventy-five per cent of the purchases it shall not apply at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has overlooked the fact that by the action of this House, whether he agrees with the conclusion or not, it was decided that the operation of the Government railways should be carried on under one unified system. That system will include the Intercolonial, and the Canadian Northern, and the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. We will have a national system of railways of approximately 22,000 miles in length with the associated steamship services. The whole operation of the system will be carried on. by a responsible board of management. In carrying on the operation of that ,whole system under the board of management, the purchase of supplies becomes part of the necessary work and operation of that system. The work of the purchasing commission does not include the purchases for the operation of the Government railways. It never has. These purchases have been made by the railways themselves. The present board of management of the railways are making the purchases for the railways through their regular purchasing departments just as the Canadian Pacific makes its purchases through its own purchasing department. As I understand, the purchasing department of the

Canadian National Railway system will be exactly The same in its general scope and the character of its work as the purchasing department of the Canadian Pacific.
With this very big difference that in one case the board of directors are shareholders in the company and in the other they are not; so that the control is quite different.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What my hon. friend says applies to the whole operation of the Government system of railways. It does not apply merely to the purchase of supplies. The question is an important one, we have debated it in the House before, and I do not wish to enter into a discussion of it at the present time. That is agreed.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is agreed. The purchase of supplies for these railways is a necessary part of the work of the board of management.
