The other portion of the purchasing, that is of supplies for the Government departments is what is covered by this resolution.

As I understand my hon. friend's remarks they are to be interpreted in this way: The Canadian National Railway purchases are to be made absolutely irrespective of politics but is not to be the system of purchasing for the rest of the departments. Is that what he means?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I mean and say quite the contrary. I said that,the railway supplies were to be purchased by the railway management free from political suggestion and we are providing that the supplies in the other departments are to be purchased equally and wholly free from polities and purchased by tender in the manner provided by this resolution. There is this difference and it is introduced in deference to the view expressed in Parliament; the chairman of this board will be a member of the Government. When a similar measure was before the House last session ob-
*:T
jection was taken that there was no direct link between the commission and the Government. That objection has been removed and provision has been made by .this legislation that the chairman of the commission shall be a rpember of the Privy Council. He does not receive any salary as chairman of the board. He will be a minister presiding over one of the other departments and his compensation as minister of that other department will cover any service that he renders under this resolution.

I can readily understand why there should be a purchasing commission for the Railway, Marine and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment departments where there are many millions of dollars being spent, but if it is necessary to have a purchasing commission for these large spending departments I do not see any wisdom in having such a commission to do the purchasing for the small spending departments. The hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution told us that these supplies would be advertised for. I understand that is the rule now. I am a believer in a democratic government and in a democratic people and I think there is too much taken out of the hands of the Parliament of Canada now. A by-word throughout the Dominion of Canada tojday is that Government and Parliament have nothing to do but stand up and vote, that everything i,s handled by a commission. If there is something wrong or if there is a mistake made whom are we going to hold responsible-not the Government or Parliament but, we will say, the Civil Service Commission or the purchasing commission. Are the people of this country not to hold anybody responsible for mistakes that are made and anything improper that is done? I can quite understand the purchasing commission buying some goods and having the purchases concentrated here at Ottawa. But take the particular county of western Ontario in which I live-if some brooms or brushes and soap were needed there it would cost as much to send those articles from Ottawa as to buy them on the spot.
I am strongly opposed to anything being done, or any more commissions being appointed, that will take work out of the hands of members of Parliament. The members of the Government and the members of Parliament ought to be held responsible for all purchases that are made and all mistakes that may be committed. We know that at the present time no responsibility devolves upon members of Parliament in connection with the Civil Ser-

vice Commission. We were told at one time that three persons were to be appointed to the Civil Service 'Commission at a certain . salary. Then a year later w7e were told that three more were to be appointed at an increased salary. If that were all there would not be so much to complain of, but there is a huge staff there now.
We were told by the minister who introduced this. Bill that he is not aware that any of the staff of the present purchasing commission will be dismissed. If that is the case what does it mean? It means that we are adding to the debt of this country by every commission that we appoint. We were led to believe that the Civil Service Commission would cost about $45,000 a year, but the facts are that it is costing a couple of hundred thousand dollars a year, and it will ibe the same in the present instance. I think the Government should curb this tendency to appoint commissions. We have ministers capable of handling these matters, and now that the war is over and the departments do not have quite so much to do, I think we should allow those departments to handle the purchasing of these supplies. Surely the work done by these commissions can be placed under the control of the Government departments, so that the Government can deal with these mattters themselves and somebody be held responsible for the matter which is carried out. If there is any class of men to-day in Canada that should be qualified to purchase supplies for the Government's use, it is the men at the heads of the different departments. If this work were allotted to these men the Government and the people could hold them responsible for it. As it is now when a member of one of these commissions makes a mistake you cannot do anything with him. If a Cabinet Minister does anything blameworthy he is held responsible, and when he goes to the people for re-election they put him out, and punish him in that way. But appointments under this commission are made for a term of ten years and during that time this man can do almost what he likes.
It has been said that millions of dollars have been saved through the activities of the War Purchasing Commission. I assert that no man in this House can say and prove that $10 has been saved. I know of a case where a tender was sent in to the War Purchasing Commission, which tender was not accepted. Another contractor was awarded the contract and he bought the goods from the unsuccessful tenderer at a larger amount than the latter had tendered for to the Government, and thus 
the successful tenderer made a very large profit. I am not saying that mistakes have not been made in the past. It is human to err and therefore mistakes have been made, and I suppose will continue to be made. But I firmly believe we ought to hold the Government-no matter what party is in office-responsible, and not appoint a commission involving a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars, in order to get somebody a nice fat job, especially when it'is not possible to bring home responsibility to him. I repeat that in my opinion every department of Government ought to be held responsible for its own purchases.
I cannot understand the selection of three men to make purchases for so many different departments, especially when the purchases cover such a wide variety of articles. I do not think there is a company or a corporation in Canada that would send a watchmaker to buy boots and shoes, or a shoeman to purchase watches, -drugs, or commodities of that nature. Yet in this case three men are to be assigned to the task of making these purchases. Why not let the officials of each department do it? They should do it, because no one man is qualified to purchase for all the public departments-that is utterly impossible. Each man knows his own department, and that is all he can, in the ordinary course of things be conversant with.
We are only adding to the existing difficulties by embarking to a further extent upon the appointment of commissions. Surely the ministers and the deputy ministers are honest enough to be entrusted with this responsibility; they have been considered so in the past. Let them see that things are done right and if the existing officials are not competent let them be replaced. Let them advertise for tenders for supplies, and require them to accept the lowest tender, if it is possible otherwise to accept it. (In that way we can hold the Government responsible for whatever is done.

I must say that I heartily agree with much of what has been said by my hon. friend from Dufferin. It does seem to me most unfortunate that the Government-after the experience they have had with the commissions that have been appointed in the past, and the consequent dissatisfaction throughout the country- should now be proposing to appoint another commission consisting of two or three men, to make the purchases for all the different public departments. It appears to. me that it is utterly impossible to get two

or three qualified men who would be conversant with the needs of all the departments and know what was best to be done so far as those departments were concerned. We have heard a great deal from the Government on the subject of economy. Would this not be a good time for the Government to take action themselves along that line, cut out such appointments as these, and allow the different departments to purchase what they need as they did in days gone by. Let the Government do that and not create more positions, doubtless positions of a really soft character, for some friends who want to get a job and hang on to it at the expense of the country.
The question was raised a few minutes ago as to whether this commission would make purchases for the 'Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. In this connection arises whether the members of this commission would have the special knowledge as to the requirements, for example, of those soldiers who are taking up farming as a profession. Another question that presents itself is whether these men will be qualified to purchase the seed grain that is needed. I doubt very much if the Government will show good judgment if they attempt to pass this resolution and force upon Parliament the appointment of these men. In my opinion it will only give rise to a lot of trouble. Perhaps we on this side should not worry very much about that but nevertheless I think the Government are only getting into a lot of difficulty which they would escape if they left this matter alone. As the hon. gentleman (,Mr. Best) has stated the heads of departments should be responsible for the purchasing of supplies that are needed. At present there seems to be an entire absence of responsibility. That is illustrated by the answer to an inquiry which was made the other day by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert). The answer was, with reference to the matter in question, that the Government knew nothing about it. By such a procedure as is now proposed the Government are simply shirking responsibility. The only satisfaction the people get out of it is that they have to pay these large salaries when money is needed for vastly more important purposes.

I would suggest to the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) that if he had taken the trouble to visit the offices of the commission and ascertained what their course of procedure is, and what they are doing, he would not have spoken as he
did. I have taken that trouble. I went to the offices of the War Purchasing Commission and investigated their work.
I can only hear every third word the hon. gentleman is saying.
If the hon. gentleman will keep quiet, I will guarantee that my voice will carry across the Chamber.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster) is getting his money's worth even at that.
Mr. BLAKE;: I have investigated the War Purchasing Commission's work and their manner of letting contracts, and how they disposed of the surplus material left with the Militia Department after the war was over. In every case I investigated I found that the commission obtained full value for the goods that were disposed of. There was, for example, the disposition of motor cars. The city of Winnipeg municipal hospitals wished to purchase two motor cars, but were disputing the price on the ground that it was too high. I went into the facts and I was quite satisfied that the Government was getting a very good price for the motor car and I could not see that there was any bargain in it for the hospital people.
This War Purchasing Commission has also had on its hands the disposition of surplus stock bought from time to time by the various departments of the Government, some of which stock had lain in store for probably twenty years. That only goes to show how criminally extravagant were the persons who heretofore looked after the purchasing of our supplies. I am satisfied that the War Purchasing Commission has saved this country millions of dollars not only in the purchasing of supplies during the war, but in the disposal of surplus stocks after the war.
I am satisfied that the principle of establishing a commission which will do the purchasing for all the departments of the government service is right and will work out satisfactorily in practice. For example, with a purchasing board, if a department wants a certain line of supplies, it will have to furnish specifications and those specifications will be checked and advertised, samples will be procured, and the delivered goods will have to measure up to those samples. In that way it does not matter whether even a watchmaker is buying the goods; it is simply a question of follow ing the specifications and seeing that the articles measure up to those specifications.

If hon. members will investigate the War Purchasing Commission I am satisfied they will be unanimous in the opinion that the establishment of this hoard will be a good thing for the country.
Did the hon. member investigate the re-sale in the West of cavalry saddles?

I am informed that some of those saddles were bought twenty-two years ago, so it can be seen how extravagant the purchases were in those days. I really have not gone into' the matter raised by my hon. friend.

If the hon. member for
Winnipeg thinks the Purchasing Commission to be appointed under this resolution will be so effective that it will save millions of dollars to this country, does he not think the Government might extend the same principle to the purchase of railway and marine supplies?
And save more money.
That is a matter of-
Policy.

Not of policy, but a matter of great magnitude. With our railways spread all over the Dominion, it is almost impossible for the purchasing of supplies to be directed from Ottawa. I am satisfied that the man in charge of a division on a railway should be responsible for that division's needs. A man who runs a foundry in Winnipeg informed me that all the castings for shoe brakes are made in Hamilton and are then hauled to Winnipeg and western points, so that in the long run they cost really as much as if they had been cast at Winnipeg at a slightly higher price. I think that opens up the desirability of our having confidence in the men at the head of our Railways and Mercantile Marine, and if we have confidence in them, I see no reason why they should not he allowed to do their purchasing through their own organizations.	-
Does the hon. .member believe in doing away with the Public Accounts Committee?
Not at all.
Well, with the establishment of this board the Public Accounts Committee would be of no use.
Why not?

Because all the
purchases will not come before the Public Accounts Committee.
'Sir GEORGE FOSTER: Why not?

This board will
be responsible.

But every account will be audited. The Auditor General's report goes before the Public Accounts Committee and is the subject of review and examination by that committee. My hon. friend is entirely wrong in thinking that this is a contrivance to withdraw this expenditure from review either by the Auditor General or the Public Accounts Committee.

But if we have
any criticism about some purchases the answer of the Government will be that this board is responsible.
'Sir GEORGE FOSTER:	But my hon.
friend must be fair about this matter. The 'Government will be responsible, for a member of the Government sitting in this House will be Chairman of the Commission.

That does not
make any difference.

Will the minister explain the meaning of paragraph 5 of the resolution? If I understand it rightly, it means that any department that wishes to buy anything will buy through the board, that the board will send estimates to the Governor in Council, that the Governor in Council will approve of those estimates, and then the purchase will be made. But will any estimates be brought down by the several departments before the House of Commons as is done now?

I explained that very carefully in my previous remarks. Under the commission as i't exists to-day, and under the commission as it will exist if this Bill passes, the responsibility of every department for the (quantity, the quality, the variety and the nature of its supplies is thrown upon itself, - and the (commission buys not a single ounce of anything 'for a department except on requisition by the department itself. So that tlpe ministerial responsibility is kept, in the first place, in each ministerial head of the department, and he is responsible before the Public Accounts Committee and before this House for every article that he has allowed to be requisitioned for his department.

Then if I understand the hon. Acting Prime Minister rightly, the system rwill be very defective. Suppose the Minister of Public Works foresees that for the coming year he will need a certain amount of supplies, he will put in the Estimates an amount to cover the value of those supplies, $200,000, $500,000, or $1,000,000. The moment that money is voted by Parliament what discretion does the board exercise, and how can it economize when the money is already voted? The practice in the various departments is at present uniform and Parliament can curtail the expenditure of any department.

The very same responsibility in both measure and kind *will exist as would exist if there were no purchasing commission.
Mr. 'CANNON: Suppose the Minister of Public Works has a sum of $1,000,000 for the purchase of suppli&s, can the purchasing board prevent that minister spending the money if he so wishes?

A minister comes down, commission or no commission, and he asks the House for $1,000,000 for certain purposes of expenditure, he gets that from Parliament, and' he is responsible for the useful and economical administration and 'expenditure of that money. The fact that he has got $1,000,000 from Parliament as no. warrant to him to squander the money,-to spend it uselessly, inefficiently or otherwise; he is held responsible for that, and he is held responsible in exactly the same way if he purchases through the purchasing commission. It is he who has to authorize the requisition, to say whether he wants this thing or that thing, of this quality or of that quality, and he does not shift, and cannot shift, that responsibility on to a purchasing commission or any one else.
But has the responsible minister anything to sav about the price of the article which he has requisitioned?

He will have just what he has now. This is the general principle which applies now:	The minister
makes up his mind as to what he wants. He does not immediately fix a price; he goes to the supplying public. He makes his specifications, provides for his inspection and calls for tenders. Of these the minister is bound to take the lowest, unless there is some very strong reason why he should not do so. The principle followed in connection with the purchasing of supplies by this commission will be exactly the same.

Will it be exactly the same. At present the minister has the determination of prices, .because if the price is too high he may refuse to buy. In this case, unless he happens to be the minister presiding over the commission, he will have no voice in fixing the price. I quite agree that he will be responsible up to the point of ordering the goods, but having requested the purchasing commission to supply the goods, he immediately loses all control.

But the control is there in the interests of the public. What is the commission appointed for? To purchase on clear specifications, in accordance with requisitions made by any department of the Government or by any minister. There are to be specifications; there is to be inspection; the purchase must be by tender and contract. The minister is more than protected. He is in a better position than he was before, because he is protected by a commission of three, one of the members of which is a member of the Government.
He hides behind the commission.
Does my hon. friend call it hiding?

When my right hon. friend says that the position of the minister under this proposal will be the same as it has been I think he is mistaken. The minister has the control of the price, but under this proposal he will lose that control. Possibly there will be another control which will be effective; I am not arguing that. The minister loses all control once he gives the order to the commission.

The minister retains that control which it is in the public interest to retain. I have been a minister for many years, and so has my hon. friend. I have had a long experience with reference to the purchasing of supplies for different departments of the Government. This commission will be appointed for ten years. It will have no other object than that of purchasing all the goods that it is asked to purchase according to specifications. The members of the commission will specialize in that work. They will buy in large quantities; they will do away with competition between the departments in the purchasing of similar lines of goods. The hand of the minister is strengthened by the fact that the business of purchasing goes into the

hands of a commission which has a minister as its chairman. The _ member for West Kenit (Mr. MeCoig) is, I am quite certain, a business man. He will realize that in view of the requirements of so large and varied a service as the public service of Canada, with its purchases amounting to from $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 a year, the ministers themselves whose duties are multitudinous, cannot, even with the help of their staffs, get the best articles at the best prices, with the best inspection and the best return for the money expended, as readily as a commission instituted as this is. It will be the sole duty of this commission to attend to purchases. They will become experts in that business. They will come to know all the sources of supply; they will buy in bulk; they will have the whole market at their hand. My hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) has made two or three statements to-day. We all have the liberty of expressing our views, and for the statements that we make we draw upon our information and our experience. Well, I draw from my experience. During the last five or six years I have observed very closely the operations of the purchasing commission. The member for West Kent says that we are appointing another commission, giving fat jobs to the people who need them-some of our favourites, maybe, or something like that. But we have a purchasing commission now; we have had it for five years. We are not adding to the number of commissions; we are simply following along the line of experience. I had something to do with attempting to purchase supplies for war purposes during the first two years of the war, and it is my opinion, based on close observation, that during the last five years we have saved millions of dollars as the result of having this commission purchase our supplies. I honestly believe that; if I did not, I would not be so strongly in favour of a commission. We have keen business men in this committee, on both sides; I appeal to them as to whether the principle is sound. Some one says: If the principle is good, why not apply it to the operation of the Government railways? Well, it is applied in connection with purchases for the T\niwayS. No great railway system would ei it fpr five years if it had not a purchasing department equal in efficiency and thoroughness to the purchasing departments maintained by its competitors. No commercial distributing house carrying on a large business continues the old haphazard system of buying in detail here and there in preference to the system 
of purchasing through a properly equipped . purchasing department. That is the only way you can carry on big businesses to-day, and our railway system, be it large or small, must have that efficient factor in its administration if it is to be successful and to meet its competitors. The Government is simply continuing a principle that has been found to give good results during the last five years; simply asking the committee to give to this purchasing commission a further lease of life so that the same good work may be accomplished in the future as has been accomplished in the past.

I can readily see the advantage of having the purchasing operations of the Government centralized, because it would be folly for, say five men from five different departments to go and buy five desks. What I do not like about this proposal is the establishment of a commission. If it be desirable to have the purchasing operations consolidated-and I am inclined frankly to say that I believe that is desirable-the Government having met the objection which others and myself voiced very strongly the session before last when this matter was brought up, namely, that there should be a minister at the head, might the Government not still go further and propose this to the House? If it be desirable to have the purchasing operations consolidated, let a minister be placed at the head; then let him take by transfers from other departments those men who at present through their experience are skilled in purchasing and have knowledge of the necessities of their different departments, and let them be grouped under the minister. I believe in responsible government; I believe we 'Should have in this House a minister who will explain to us, if needs be, the actions, not of a man over whom he has no control, a man appointed at a salary for ten years, but of one of his -I might use the word "underlings," and I use it in no sense of disrespect-subordinates

that is the word for which I am seeking. If it be desirable to have this purchasing activity consolidated, it should be consolidated under a minister of the Crown, and all the staff in that department should be under the minister just in the same way as other permanent officials are under the ministers of the different departments. That is a suggestion which I would recommend to the Government for adoption. It is sound, and I do not think it in any way affects the objects which the Government say they have in view in introducing this legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should like to endorse what my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) has just said. In that connection,
I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) if he has considered the possible embarrassments, difficulties and complications that might arise in the event of a minister of the Crown differing from his two colleagues who are permanent appointees. I can imagine a situation in which my right hon. friend might take a view very different from that of his two colleagues who had been permanently appointed. In what position would he then be placed? Would he have to defend in Parliament an action on the part of the board to which he, as minister of the Crown, wras opposed and which he thought unwise? If he is not to take that position, what position is tliere left for him to take? That seems to open the door to destroying altogether ministerial responsibility,-to leave it to the minister to come down to the House and say: I, as a member of the Government, have disagreed with the whole purchase that has been made; but the majority of the board has ruled and the permanent members of the commission have so decided, and I have, therefore, no choice but to voice the decision of the commission. A few minutes ago an hon. member spoke about the minister hiding behind the commission, and very strong exception was taken to that statement. If a minister of the Crown said in this House that he had disagreed with his colleagues, but his colleagues had thought well to take such and such a course, he would simply be hiding behind his colleagues. As t!he resolution is framed now, the door is left open to the Government to do what-5 p.m. ever it pleases in the matter of purchasing. When it wishes to make a purchase, if it does not desire to assume full responsibility for that purchase, the minister's colleagues can make the purchase and then the minister can say that he was opposed to it. On the other hand when something is done that meets with public approval, the minister can take full credit for it. We are getting far away from ministerial responsibility, and the suggestion made that a minister of the Crown should take the responsibility of centralizing the purchasing work, but should centralize it in a department for which he would be responsible and for which he would have to give an account in all its details on the floor of this House, is much more in accord with the idea of responsible government and with what are the rightful
privileges of Parliament in the matter of criticism.

It is open to any person to conjure up difficulties that might arise in carrying out any scheme of operation. Contingencies may arise, but a great deal of what my hon. friend has' suggested is fanciful and it it not necessary that it' should originate in or grow up out of this scheme of administration. Let us take one very reasonable answer to my hon. friend's t suggestion. For two or three years a member of the Government was on that purchasing commission, and along with him on the same commission were two other gentlemen.
I refer to Sir Edward Kemp, and from the time that Sir Edward Kemp and his colleagues undertook that work of the purchasing commission, no such contingency as my hon. friend suggests arose. They are business men; they are not playing politics on that commission; there is not the struggle for a vote from this section or influence from another section. These two men are on that commission to carry out a business operation on business principles, and being sensible business men, they agree as a rule; if they do not agree .at first, after conferring with one another, they come to an agreement. But what are the things about which they might disagree? The principle of ten-dor and contract is laid down and they know the goods that are requisitioned for, so that they could not disagree about that. The minister from the other department puts in his requisition, and those three men on the commission have to sit down and consider how they will best get those goods along the line of tender and contract. There is no opportunity for differing as to the wideness with which tenders shall be called for. Under the present purchasing commission, everybody has the right to have his name put upon the list and to be consulted when goods are wanted, and tenders are to be called for them. There could not be any difficulty there. There is no opportunity for the members of the commission quarrelling one with another in regard to the specifications; those are technical matters and the specifications are worked out as to the kinds and qualities of goods. If you take the matter and reason it out from one thing to another, where is this big bogey that the minister may have some internal conflict with the other two members which may result in a sanguinary manner or which may result in a manner which is even worse than sanguinary, where one man chooses to hide behind another? Those are fanciful things, I think. Certainly they have not

cropped up in the experience of the commission while Sir Edward Kemp was its head, and I do not think they need be very much apprehended now. As regards ministerial responsibility, what does my hon. friend want? He wants to go back to the old system-

Hear, hear; it is all
right.

-of patronage, pure and gimple, to have nothing but a political bureau with a political man at the head of it. In his view a minister of the Crown should be at the head of it; and he alone should have the final say with reference to the whole matter; he may have subordinates, but they are not his equals; they are absolutely his subordinates and under his control and command. Will he be likely to get as good, honest co-operation and advice in that way as he would when two business men were working along with him? I . do not think so.
Better.

In the other case it becomes simply the old political department witlh a member of the Cabinet responsible for buying all the supplies that are needed. What happens when you have a political head? Immediately pressure is put upon him. My hon. friends who have been in 'Cabinets know what that means, and what it will mean in the future. This proposition has been worked out from experience, with a view to devising a business method for getting supplies that will enable us to get away as far as possible-absolutely away, I believe-from political or partisan influence that would direct when and how and from whom supplies should be bought. This is bringing it down to a business basis. Three men, I think, are better than one. You will still have your ministerial responsibility, because one of the members of the board will be a member of the Privy Council.

It is pleasing to learn that there has been such an amiable disposition on the part of the War Purchasing Commission, but we have no guarantee that we shall always have such a pleasant and amiable person as Sir Edward Kemp at its head. Where is the bogey in what the leader of the Opposition has suggested? Here is a proposal to create a board that shall have exclusive power to purchase things and to engage in large operations.
I need not go into the details, but that board must do certain things, and there are ' 
certain things that cannot be done without the approval of the board. What does that mean? The board, whenever it is mentioned, must mean a majority of the board. What else can it mean? There is no suggestion here that the minister has any power independent of the board. He is chairman of a board of three, and it is quite conceivable that the other two members of the board appointed for a period oi ten years, and with probably a permanent tenure of office, may sometimes differ from the minister. Bet me just give a possible case. Notwithstanding what we say about the abolition of patronage, it is quite possible that two of the members of the board who are to be appointed under this Act, if it shall become an Act, will be friends of the present Government. I only suggest that as a possibility, but it is a possibility.
They would not be any the worse for that.
The board would be open to suspicion in the country.

These gentlemen hold
office for ten years. Now I state another possibility. It is possible that in a long short of ten years there may be a change of government; it is just possible that there may be a change within two years' time. Again, I am putting it very mildly. With a change of government we will have a minister associated with these two gentlemen who would be of a different shade of political colour, and you might not have the same amiable relations as prevailed between Sir Edward Kemp and the gentlemen who have honoured us by serving us-and I am not questioning for a moment their efficiency. You are going to have on the board twTo gentlemen appointed by the present Government, and before many months are over, in all probability, at all events it is a possibility, a minister who will not be in sympathy with them. Now then, there being a reasonable possibility of a difference of opinion between these gentlemen, how are they going to decide in any other way than by a majority vote? What other way is there? There is more than a possibility, there is every probability, that the difficulties suggested by the leader of the Opposition will occur. The board will be paralysed by a difference of opinion, and if the Government say "This is a board that is absolutely independent, there is the law," a minister of the 'Crown may be held responsible for that with which he has nothing to do. I do not think that the point raised by the leader of the Opposition is a bogey at all; it is a grim reality.

At the first flush this looks like a very good business proposition, but I think I recognize in it a similarity to the Bill which was brought in by my hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) two sessions ago, and which had rather a rocky passage part way through the 'House. While the arguments used by the leader of the Government, commend themselves to my mind in some respects, I do not think this legislation in its working out will bring nearly the good results that are expected of it. Think of the variety of the supplies that will have to be purchased for use in different parts of the country, and which will have to be delivered to a thousand different points. I foresee in the first place that this is going to centralize purchasing in the same way that the Civil Service Commission has centralized appointments; that is evident on the face of it, and we know that when anything is centralized in Ottawa it means the cutting out of the smaller and even the bigger towns remote from the capital to a considerable extent.
That may possibly save some money, but the policy that has been pursued in this country, and I think with fairly good results, has been to buy supplies for the public service at the point at which delivery was required. I do not know what the exact figures are, but I suppose we burn half a million tons of coal in the public buildings in Canada per annum. That amount has to be distributed all over this Dominion. Is it the intention that simply one block order shall be given for half a million tons of coal to meet the requirements of the public service in Canada? The minister has not explained that, and it appears to me that these questions will press for solution when it comes to the Act. I just want to guard the minister against possible error if he thinks that a great saving can be made by centralizing all the goods purchased at one point and then distributing them all over Canada.

So that my hon. friend need not pursue an argument on a basis which I do not think is a proper one, let me say that the Government has not the least idea that the board will purchase all the supplies and store them at Ottawa, for instance, or any other place, in some building, from which they will be distributed as required. That would be the opposite of economy in a country like ours.

a success it does not follow that a purchasing board to purchase the supplies required in all the districts, towns and cities from Vancouver to Halifax is going to be a like success. I cannot see it. Every one who knows anything about agencies knows that the big institutions with 300 or 400 agencies scattered throughout the country, and particularly in the West, allow these agencies to purchase supplies for their focal requirements. I do not think that is had business, I think it is the right kind pf business and that it will commend itself to the judgment of those who think the matter over. While the purchasing of large supplies should not go through the departments, and the departments want to get rid of it bedause it has been a source of trouble in the past, and while I sympathize with what the minister says in that respect at the same time I believe it will uot bring the saving to this country that is expected and I fear that if there is not some better ground for it than the minister has adduced-and he has adduced very jnany fine arguments-there will be a rocky road ahead for this measurfe the same as there was when it was sponsored by the President of the Privy Council two sessions ago. It was pretty fully discussed and the same objections that existed then exist inow. I believe that centralization should not be carried to an extreme and that local requirements should be left to local merchants and manufacturers.
' Mr. JACOBS: I agree with every word which has fallen from the hon. member [DOT]for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). When this /resolution was before this House last *session it was in charge of the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) but the Government found the going rather heavy and there has been a change of generalship. It was found that the Bill could not possibly go through under the leadership of the President of the Privy Council and now the father, or head of the family finding it was not child's play has taken hold of it in the hope that it will be more successful. I cannot understand /What object the Government has in attempting to force this Bill through an unwilling Parliament. No person seems to be in favour of it with the possible exception of the minister, and his colleague of last year, who had it in hand. We have been told by several ministers who spoke on the question last year, and I think today, although I was not in the House, that .millions and tens of millions of dollars were saved to the country through the 
operation of the War Purchasing Board. Why was it that these large sums of .money were saved to the country by the War Purchasing Board? If the War Purchasing Board were able to save this money why should not the ministers, each in his department, have saved this large sum? If the ministers are not able to purchase these supplies and to save money why do they not resign with good grace and allow .the members of the War Purchasing Com-,mission to take their places? It would be a splendid thing if we could save the money that we need so badly. I cannot congratulate the right hon. the Acting , Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) on his left-handed [DOT]allusion to the deputy ministers. He .stated that it would be impossible for the deputy ministers to do as well as this new commission which is going to be brought into life. He also said .that they are going to be licked into shape at some time in the future, that when they are so licked into shape they would have as much experience as the deputy ministers and that they were going to do better than the deputy ministers could. I have enough confidence in the capacity and ability of the deputy ministers to believe that they are quite capable of handling their own departments. The ministers themselves have very little knowledge of their departments, they are shifted around from one to the other like the bobbin on a weaving machine. The hon. gentleman who is now acting Minister of Public Works was formerly Minister of Customs and is now Minister of Railways and Canals. In the last six months we have had the Department of Public Works under no. fewer than three ministers and the end i.s not yet The poor overloaded minister who already had the Department of Railways and Canals on his hands-and surely that is enough work for a big man-was placed in charge of the Department of Public Works. How can a man handle the Department of Railways and Canals and the Department of Public Works at the same time and give satisfaction to the country? It is impossible. They rely upon the deputy ministers to look after the departments because these know all about the technical details of the administration. The ministers are mere figureheads, they are here to answer questions, to give the answers which are put into their mouths by the deputies sitting on the floor of the House. When we have deputy ministers who are qualified by years of service in their departments, why should we want to take the purchasing of

supplies out of their hands and give it not only possibly but probably to men who never purchased a dollars' worth of supplies in their lives? It is not for me to suggest to the Government what they ought to do under the circumstances. We see insurrection on all sides. They cannot hope to have any support from this side of the House because we believe that this Bill is bad in essence and we find important defections already on the part of a number of hon. gentlemen on the other side. Last year this Bill was withdrawn, I believe, as a result of the very effective address which was delivered by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Stewart), who does not sit on this side of the House. Why in the name of Heaven will the Government persist in forcing this Bill down our throats' when we do not want it? The conduct of the Government in this matter leads me to believe in the old saying that whom the gods wish to destroy they first make mad.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sure the House appreciates the solicitude of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) who has just taken his seat for the men on this side and his sympathy is very cordially reciprocated. I may make one or two observations, not so much in reference to what the hon. member has said because I cannot congratulate him on this occasion on making gny important or valuable contribution to the discussion- he has not illuminated the subject by any of those flashes of genius which occasionally interest and entertain the House-but in reference to the remarks of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) he has assumed that the Bill proposes or contemplates a situation which is not in contemplation at all. It never has been suggested-it was not suggested last year-it is not suggested now-that everything should be purchased and assembled here in Ottawa and distributed all over the country. That question came up last year, and was discussed in -the House. As a matter of fact the purchasing today is done, as it has always been done, from Ottawa, in the sense that the final authority rests in this city. If there was no purchasing body at all, the final authority is the minister; the authority proceeds from Ottawa, wherever the purchase is made, no matter what the purchasing body is. It is not the fact, as my hon. friend has suggested, that the purchases of the War Purchasing Commission have been confined to war supplies, although that was the case until January 1918. About that time-I forget the exact date-the scope of the work of the commission was enlarged so as to cover the purchase of supplies for all the Government departments, apart from the Government Railway system. Since then the purchasing of supplies for all the departments has been under the supervision of the commission. Has there been the centralization, which my hon. friend fears, during the past fifteen months in connection with its work? I venture to think there has not been that centralization. Then, if there has not been centralization during the past fifteen months, what ground is there for fear at the present time? The whole object of the Bill, as already outlined by the Acting Prime Minister, is to give the country, in the future, the benefit of the experience and knowledge accumulated during the last five years in improved methods of purchasing government supplies, with the additional advantage that the board will make the purchases, instead of merely supervising them, thereby securing a greater degree of efficiency than has been possible under the existing system. My hon. friend is one of the ablest business men in the House, and he knows that in the purchase of supplies of any kind the knowledge of the purchaser is a most important factor in getting value for the money. There is not a large institution in Canada purchasing large quantities of supplies that does not consider the man who makes the purchases one of the most important of its staff. No single man, perhaps-unless it be the head of the organization himself-can contribute more to the financial success of that organization than the purchasing agent who knows the value of goods and sees that he does not pay more than those goods are worth. I will give one illustration-I cannot state the precise details from memory -which came under my observation where some supplies were advertised for. Tenders came in, but the prices received indicated that the tenderers asked more than the market price of the goods. This was apparent because it is the duty of the board to keep in touch with the market price. The board must know the specifications and be familiar with the quality of the goods, so that if a tender does come in for articles of any particular class which is above the current market price, that immediately becomes a matter of inquiry forthwith. Thus the knowledge the board have accumulated and the experience they have gained in carrying on this work, week after week, month after month, can be applied to every transaction that comes before them. Accordingly if they find that

tenderers are asking more than the current market price, they can decline to accept those offers, and can call for new tenders in order that they may get the goods, at such current market price. Therefore in the purchase of supplies, a knowledge on the part of the purchasers of what the current prices are, is one of the most important factors in the situation.
Now let me deal with the suggestion that the deputy ministers of the various departments, should perform this duty. The deputy ministers have their time so taken up with the routine and other business of their departments, that they cannot pretend to keep posted on the current prices of all the classes of commodities which may be required by their departments. Nor can any minister, with the duties which devolve upon him, pretend to keep in touch with the current market price of all the commodities that his department may require. It is true that if the head of a department happened to be a business man, and thoroughly familiar with certain lines of industry, he would probably be accurately informed and would be able to judge whether the prices asked for the goods with which he was familiar were the current market prices, but another minister might not have that knowledge. There is this great difference between the two systems you have actual expert knowledge applied to the actual conditions of purchasing in the one case as compared with knowledge that cannot he expert from the very nature of the system under which the purchasing is being done.

Would the minister explain, with respect to the item of coal that I mentioned, how the Purchasing Commission would proceed? Where this coal was wanted in every city from Victoria to Halifax, and, say 500,000 tons, were required, would the commission buy the coal and distribute it to all those different centres?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I assume that it would be done in the future exactly as it has been done in the past.
Then that is all right.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because we have had an independent commission supervising it. My understanding is that the commission call for tenders for the delivery of coal in the particular centres where the coal is required. If coal is wanted, for example, in Winnipeg, they cal! for the delivery of so1 much coal in that city, and the same as re-
gards the various centres throughout the country.
That is just as it has been done in the past.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is not that satisfactory?
It is quite satisfactory. That is the system I want continued.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not understand that in a matter of that kind there would be any difference whatever. But when you come to deal with the different departments in Ottawa you may have half a dozen departments requiring the same class of supplies. Then, is it a wise thing to buy in bulk for all the departments in Ottawa at the best price you can get, or is it better to have half a dozen departments competing against each other, buying in smaller quantities the same class of supplies that are needed here? That is the question, and I submit that no business man. who gives the matter careful consideration can reach any conclusion other than it is wise, that it is true economy, and in the public interest to adopt the course of action the Government has resolved on. It is because of the actual experience gained-which the Acting Prime Minister has already referred to-that the Government is of opinion that this Bill is greatly in the public interest.
My hon. friend referred to the introduction of this measure'last year. It was the Prime Minister's Bill last year though he asked me to take charge of it. It was the Prime Minister's desire a year ago that the Bill should go through. No man in this House spoke more strongly in support of the Bill than the Prime Minister himself when he returned from France. At that late period of the session the Prime Minister did not consider it expedient to press the Bill through, but he intimated at the time that, while he withdrew the measure he would be glad to receive any suggestions in reference to its form and the matter would be dealt with at a later session. The Acting Prime Minister has properly brought in the Bill which is at present before the House pursuant to the promise of the Prime Minister made when he withdrew the Bill almost a year ago.. There is this important change in the Bill, a member of the Government will be chairman of the board. The main ground of criticism-or at least one of the main grounds of criticism-from certain hon. members at that time was that they claimed there was no direct connection between the Government and the work of this board, and therefore there was a lack of

ministerial responsibility for it. The Prime Minister controverted that proposition by stating clearly and frankly that the Government could not escape responsibility for the work of such a board, that the Government that constituted that board must accept responsibility for its acts. But in order to make clear beyond peradventure the responsibility of the Government in the matter, the Bill has been amended so as to provide that the chairman of this board shall be a member of the Government. In that way we have direct governmental responsibility and we combine the two essentials: The concentration of the work of purchasing supplies in the hands of men who make that their only business, and whose only purpose is to secure the best value for the public money expended, coupled with responsibility of the Government for the work of the board by the chairman being a member of the Government. I submit that this change removes what was considered a year ago by some members to be an objection and gives us the benefit of the two principles I h ive mentioned. It will mean beyond question a very large saving to the people of Canada in the purchase of the supplies that this country requires.

Why are two commissioners needed?
Mr. ROWELL-. Well, my hon. friend might ask that question in reference to a great many phases of activity. I do not know that it is an essential feature of the Bill, but there are three commissioners now and it is considered desirable that two commissioners should be appointed in addition to the member of the Government, because there will be abundance of work for them to attend to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are there not at the present time men in the Civil Service of very wide experience in this work of purchasing commodities, and who are giving their whole time to that work and have been so doing for years past? If there are, -wdiy should they not be placed in a department together under the charge of a minister and the work concentrated? If the minister is unwilling to permit them to be associated in this work, it would appear that the real motive for this Bill is rather to provide positions for two individuals

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I must express my surprise that the hon. leader of the Opposition, with a sense of the responsibility which should characterize my hon. friend in the position he holds, should suggest that the 95
Government would introduce this Bill for the purpose of providing positions for two men. If my hon. friend wishes to be taken seriously in this House he must" refrain from making suggestions of that kind.
-Some hon. MEMBERS: Shame.
Have you got any better argument?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would go further and say to my hon. friend that the fact that we have at the present time officers in the permanent service who have been devoting their time for years past to this class of work, and that he is unwilling to employ them in these positions, tends to confirm what I have said. Let me follow what I have just said by adding that I think another factor to be taken into consideration in connection with appointments of this kind is that the Government has reached a stage in the confidence of the people where it should refrain from constituting any more commissions or making any life appointments. I think the government can well afford to leave to one side further apointments of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have nothing to retract.
Of course. _
Shame.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Have you got any better argument?

Where does the
shame come in?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Some people cannot see that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Any hon. member who says that the Government has introduced this Bill for the purpose of creating two positions in the public service shows a lack of sense of responsibility which I do not think hon. members should show in dealing with matters of this kind. There may be differences of opinion about the Bill, honest differences of opinion-and I am not questioning that there are honest differences on matters of principle-but the Government has introduced this Bill solely because it believes it to be in the public interest. There is nothing in the Bill precluding the appointment of the men whom my hon. friend has referred to. The fact



is to-day that of the two commissioners of the War Purchasing Commission one has been the purchasing agent in the Department of Militia and Defence for a number of years-
Who is he?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. H. W. Brown.
Did he buy the Macadam shovel?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-and the other is the man who has been for some time acting secretary of the commission, Mr. W. S. Leckie.
If iit is deemed to be in the public interest as it is that men of experience and knowledge should be eligible for the position, there. is no reason why these men should not be eligible for appointment to these positions and they are eligible. The question is: Who are the best men for the positions in the interests of the public in view of the work they have to do? If this Government had no other object than creating two new positions in the public service, it certainly does not display very great skill in going to all this trouble to do so. If that is all the Government had in view it could accomplish the purpose in a very much easier way and with far less trouble to itself, to the House and to the country. The sole desire of the Government is to get the best possible results. The establishing of such a purchasing, board as is now proposed means the eliminating of the petty patronage that has in the past crept into the purchasing of Government supplies. No hon. member questions that statement. I know the condition that existed here when my political friends were in power, I know the patronage that existed in the purchasing of supplies as a lawyer practising my profession.
What "friends'5 does the hon. minister mean?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I want to make clear in any distinction I draw that it would not be my hon. friend because I do not want to be taken as sharing his views on public questions affecting this country.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I refer to Sir Wilfrid Laurier and to the men who were associated with him in the Government of this country. We know that was the situation. The Prime Minister stated in this House last session that that was the situation under his government in the early days of the
IMr. Rowell, i
war, and that one of the reasons for bringing about the proposed change was to eliminate that patronage. That statement will be found in Hansard. My hon. friends are not ignorant of the situation, they know what I say to be true. The whole question is: Do we want to put the purchasing of supplies on a sound business basis free from patronage in the interests of economy and of good business and for the benefit of the whole Dominion; or do we wish to return to the old conditions of party patronage which prevailed before the war under both political parties? We have the issue fairly and squarely before us and on that issue we must make a choice.

(Translation) Despite all the eloquence of the hon. President of the Privy Council, I still do not see the necessity of. supporting this resolution. Of course,, the Acting Prime Minister has just told us that the Prime Minister, ahsent on account of ill-health, would like to see this Bill go through; but the Prime Minister has been away for so long that he perhaps has had time to change his mind and I would have preferred it if the President of the Privy Council had shown us a telegram or a letter from the leader of the Government assuring us that he still is of the same mind and that he would be pleased to see this Board appointed.
The right hon. the Acting Prime Minister gave us to understand-that in the light of his own experience, he considered the appointment of this Board a very commendable thing. I entertain a great deal of respect for the experience of the hon. minister, but the present Government has committed so many blunders, has given such evidence of stupidity, that we hardly have the right to allow ourselves to be guided by the hon. gentleman's experience.
Is it not the custom for the deputy heads and the chief Clerks of the different departments to attend to whatever purchasing may be necessary in their respective departments? To-day the President of the Privy Council does not claim that these gentlemen lack the ability necessary to look after such purchases; no, he says they have not the time. In that case it should be rather easy to give them the necessary help-if their staffs should happen to be undermanned. Evidently that is not the real reason for this Bill. What the Government wants, as a certain hon. member said a few moments ago, is to incur further expense and likely to find new berths for their friends. The President of the Privy Council claims

that he does not concern himself with such trifles and that no serious-minded man would ever mention such a thing. However, the present Government has done worse things than creating two new $6,000 a year jobs for political cronies. '
I claim that such a Board would be useless. Two commissioners at $6,000 per year, would cost $12,000; but they would require offices, secretaries, stenographers, and a number of other things; before we were through we would be spending between $20,000 and $25,000 a year for this Board.
This very day I had the pleasure of meeting the Minister of Public Works; I asked him to build a wharf in my county, at a cost of a few thousand dollars. He refused, giving lack of funds as his excuse. And this same Minister favours a useless outlay of $20,000 or $25,000 a year, while he refuses to build a wharf for the farmers of the Lie-vre valley which would make it much easier for them to bring their produce to market. That is a. blunder on the part of the Government ; worse than that, I believe it shows their lack of sincerity.
I deem it my duty to protest against the expense involved in tne appointment of this Board; to my mind the money could be used to better purpose. We appoint boards every month; we have too many boards. The Board of Commerce has fallen into neglect; it couldn't do anything; thanks to political wire-pulling it's hands were tied. How do we know that these new commissioners we are asked to appoint will not be mere tools of the Government also,, operating for the protection of the Government's friends. This appears to me as an underhand move to restore patronage.
It is dear that the members of this Board will be the friends of the Government, the friends, perhaps, of the members of this House who will surely wish to favour their friends' friends.
Once more I protest against this expenditure which is useless, and unjust and is not in the best interests of the country. Let the Government look elsewhere. For instance in the city of Hull we are asking the Post Master General to increase the number of postmen so as to afford tire city proper service. We are met with a refusal and the claim that the Government has not the necessary funds. We have no money to build wharves, to increase the number of mail carriers or to fulfill any of the wants of our counties; and still the Government is trying to foist upon the country a new Board which will be absolutely useless and 95J
which will cost us thousands and thousands of dollars every year. For all these reasons I shall take pleasure in voting against this resolution.
Mr. Chairman, the President of the Council-
My hon. friend will pardon me; does he wish to debate the resolution still further?
Yes.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I propose to move that the committee rise and report progress. The Minister of Railways (Hon. J. D. Reid) is anxious to go on with the Grand Trunk Bill, the consideration of which we had set down for to-day. Now that we have had this preliminary discussion of the resolution, we may leave it for the present and take it up again on a subsequent occasion. I never was more convinced not only of the necessity but of the utility of a measure of this kind, and I propose to put my views a little more strongly even than I have before my confreres on both sides of the House, and not let the subject go until we have had a most thorough discussion of it. I invite members on both sides to make more thorough investigation of the matter and give more thorough thought to it and to what is involved in it before we come to our conclusion-because I feel that a good deal depends upon the conclusion we come to upon this measure. If any one here has time to go to the offices of the War Purchasing Commission and look over the work which is being done there-Sir Hormisdas Laporte will be glad to give the fullest information with regard to it-I think it will be well worth while.
Before the Acting Prime Minister moves that the committee rise, may I inquire when this matter will again come before the House?
I cannot tell my hon. friend, but it will come speedily before the House.	[DOT]
I suggest that the Acting Prime Minister consider the advisability of appointing a Parliamentary committee to deal with this matter and to make investigations.

WTe can consider that.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
