speechtext: If this Bill were defeated in the House, would the Government go ahead and complete the undertaking with the Grand Trunk people, or what would be the outcome?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: If this Bill were defeated in the House, what would have to be done would be this. Another agreement would have to be prepared with a new schedule, and executed. Then the Grand Trunk Railway Company would have to call another special meeting and notify all the shareholders as they did before, including the eight who were overlooked. That would make everything legal, and the Government would then proceed to take over the Grand Trunk in accordance with the Act passed last year.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Can the minister give us an estimate of what would be saved in management by amalgamating the Canadian National railways and the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member means the Grand Trunk Railway system including all the subsidiary companies. That I could hardly say. I have been taking the matter up with my officials with a view to seeing what we could save as regards the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that is a much easier matter to determine than to determine what might be saved by amalgamating the whole system. It is impossible for me to give an estimate of what the saving would be if the entire system was taken over. That is a matter of investigation; I have not undertaken to ascertain it, I could not possibly do it; but the committee that is to be appointed will endeavour 'to make all the sav-
[Sir George Foster.!
ing it can, not by amalgamating, because it cannot do that until after the award has been made, but by working the two railways together until the .award has been made. It is estimated that a very large saving will be effected if the two companies are operated together.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: About how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not a railway man and I have not had any experience in making an estimate of that kind, so that an estimate on my part would be only a guess, and I do not think it would be fair to make a guess when I have no knowledge in that regard whatever.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am sure the minister would expect us, as representatives of the people in this House, to ascertain to a fair degree of accuracy .the character of the enterprise that we are taking over. Last year, when the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Bill was before Parliament, the minister did not have any such information at hand, and he could not tell us very much laibout the standing of the main line or of its subsidiaries or branch lines. Since then he and his officials have had plenty of opportunity to asoertain what this road is earning and what its present condition is, in the main. I am not at this .stage saying that the minister should give us details of the various matters that a business man would like to know if a private concern were being taken over by him, but it will be expected that we, who sit here as representatives of the people, should know something about the property which we are buying and which is to become the property of the Canadian people. If we were isim.ply buying a pair of horses for the Government, we would have to know something about their age, theii capacity, the stock they belonged to, and we would have to make comparisons in order to find out whether we were making a good investment for the three or four hundred dollars we might invest in that simple proposition. The same principles apply here; we are buying a big railway, and 'the minister, before he asks us to confirm this bargain, should know what we are getting. For thait reason the minister should tell us the standing of those roads in the last railway year that has closed.
I do not know when the railway year closes; but if it is the same as the calendar year, the minister ought now to be able to tell us what showing the various roads that are involved in this transaction made in 1919. We had before us last session a

b-Tuebook that was handed around, one item in which showed that something in the vicinity of $2,000,000 earned in Canada had to be sent to the United States to meet deficits on the branches of this same Grand Trunk Railway system, but operating in the United States. That was a very poor showing, and it is a condition of things which the Canadian -people will' not be enamoured of. If those roads went behind last year to such an extent that that amount of money had to be sent out to keep them going, the Canadian people would like to know something about the matter. The minister ought to give us at least a general idea of this business transaction that he is putting before the House and asking us to ratify.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I take it for granted that the hon. member is asking first as to the physical condition of the Grand Trunk and its subsidiary companies. I do not think any report is published as to the physical condition of the railways of Canada. Unless some complaint is made to the Board of Railway Commissioners, the railways are supposed to be kept up by the companies in a condition that is in accordance with the law's of the country. Last year we had the statement of the president, Mr. Kelley, and other officials, that the Grand Trunk Railway system was being maintained to a standard equal to that of any other railway not only in Canada, but on the continent of America, and when we discussed the matter with the engineers of the Canadian National railways, they confirmed that statement and said that the condition of the Grand Trunk Railway system as a whole was equal to that of, say the Canadian Pacific Railway. While, perhaps, the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway system was not equal to what it was before the war, owing to war conditions, the same thing is true with regard to the Canadian Pacific and all other railways.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: They did not have so many trains and the track was as good as before.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
What I mean by my statement is this. They were not able to get rails to make renewals as they would have done in normal times; they used the rails longer so that these were not in good condition, and they were not able to keep up the standard in ties and other things. The Government were not able to investigate the books of the Grand Trunk Railway system and discuss the matter with the
officials of that company until the agreement had been signed. The agreement allowed the Government to put in officials to investigate the whole situation so that they might be prepared when the arbitration took place. We have had a staff at that work since the agreement was signed, and we expect to have all the facts necessary in order to put up our side of the case, and all information that the Grand Trunk itself would have available in this arbitration. But, of course, it will take some little time to prepare that report. As regards the financial condition of the road, that will come before the arbitrators and every side of that subject will be placed before them. The dividends, that were paid on the debenture stock and that amount to some eight or nine million dollars were paid by the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the regular way. So far as I know, their financial condition is as good this year as last, for they have been able to meet their fixed charges with the exception of the first, second and third debenture stocks.
As to the United States end of the railway, I do not know whether it will be possible for me to get a statement of the earnings for that part of the line. During the calendar year 1919 practically all the United States railways were in a sort of pooling arrangement, and the United States Government operated all the roads, guaranteeing to pay the same dividends that were paid by the several railways prior to being taken over. Of course the Grand Trunk will receive its shkre under that arrangement. So far as the Grand Trunk system as a whole is concerned I have had nothing but the most favourable reports, not by the Grand Trunk engineers alone, but by our own officials to the effect that the condition of the road is equal to that of any other railway on this continent.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister if he has seen the cablegram in to-day's Journal stating that the financial editor of the London Times thinks that in the interests of the vendors the board of arbitration should be appointed without delay. It might be as well for me to read the item and for the minister to say something about it, since the people who are making complaint stand very high in financial circles:
London, April 8.-A correspondent writes to the Times accentuating the point made by its financial editor on the delay in the appointment ot the Grand Trunk Arbitration Commission.
" Apparently it is not realized," says this correspondent, " that, assuming the award to be

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I had not seen the cablegram. I think probably the shareholders on the other side of the water hardly understand the situation. I am afraid that by some misrepresentations in the press on the other side, I do not say intentionally, a wrong impression has got abroad that we are trying to delay this matter, when as a matter of fact we are doing our best to expedite it. As I stated when introducing the Bill, a mistake was made by the Grand Trunk officials here in Canada, and in consequence two small errors in the agreement have to be corrected. In giving us a list of the companies the Grand Trunk officials omitted one railway from the schedule, and another was improperly described. That made it necessary for us either to have the agreement confirmed in this way by Parliament, or to have another meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders. The shareholders may feel that we are trying to delay the matter, but we are doing everything we can to have the agreement carried out at the earliest possible moment. I think when this Bill is passed by the House, enabling us to appoint the board of arbitrators at once, the people on the other side will be satisfied and will feel that the Government and the people of Canada are trying to carry out the agreement provided for by Parliament last session. That is one reason why, as soon as the matter has been thoroughly discussed, the Bill should be passed as speedily as possible. There is the further reason that the sooner the different re' Is are worked as one system, instead of separately, there will be, we hope, a great saving in operation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: My hon. friend understands, of course, that So far as correcting these two errors and ratifying any corrections is concerned, we on this side of the House are ready to let the Bill go through to-night to expedite matters. The only delay now is with regard to the general matter of ratification; as there is something in the Bill that we do not yet quite understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I quite understand that.
It must be remembered, however, that if the errors are not corrected in this way it will be necessary to have another meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders. That would mean sending out 70,000 notices of the calling of the meeting and probably two or three 
months further delay, during which time the shareholders would probably feel that we. were trying to raise some issue in order not to carry out the agreement. By providing for ratification in this way we are saving time, and it is not doing any injustice to the shareholders, because as I have already explained, there are only two or three who could possibly raise any objection.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Who is responsible for the mistake which makes it necessary to bring this Bill before the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company, as I explained when introducing the Bill. I then read a letter from Mr. Biggar, solicitor for the Grand Trunk, addressed to the Minister of Railways and Canals dated about a month ago, directing our attention to the fact that the schedule omitted one small line of railway three miles long, and that another railway had been described in the schedule as being held by the Grand Trunk under lease, whereas it should have been described as held by the Grand Trunk through majority stockholding' The hon. gentleman is a lawyer and will understand that in order to have clear title even to this three miles of railway, it should be mentioned in the schedule, and the particulars respecting the other line should be correctly given. After we received that letter I sent for Mr. Kelley, the president, and we took this matter up with the Deputy Minister of Justice and with the solicitors who have been engaged by that department for the arbitration. They decided that if we did not ratify the agreement in this way it would be necessary to have another meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders.
After Mr. Kelley had gone to Montreal and [DOT] consulted with their solicitors-I think they were Mr. Phippen, Mr. Atwater and Mr. Biggar-he wrote a letter to myself asking that we remedy this mistake by introducing and passing this legislation. The legislation has been introduced at the request of Mr. Kelley, President of the Grand Trunk, in order that we can get the agreement ready at the earliest possible moment.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Owing to somebody's blunder this matter has cost the country a very large sum of money and Parliament has been obliged to discuss it for the last week or ten days.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) asked the minister what would happen if this Bill were defeated and the minister said that the result would be that

we would have to enter into a new agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company because these two railways were misnamed or left out of the schedule. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said to the minister that the Opposition are prepared to accept that portion of the Bill which is designed to remedy that mistake, so that there will be no need of any further agreement with regard to these two railways. The next feature that appeals to me is this: The people, through their representatives in this Parliament, are the vendees in the present; undertaking and bargain with the Grand Trunk. A mistake has been made by the Grand Trunk shareholders or directors in calling a meeting for the ratification or confirmation of the agreement for taking over this road. As a result of that mistake some of the shareholders were * not given proper notice. Now the minister comes to this House and asks it to ratify an agreement, on behalf of the Grand Trunk Railway Company with whom we are dealing and with whom the people, whose representatives we are, are supposed to make the best possible bargain for the purchase of the road. What must the people of Canada think when they read the statements made by my hon. friend? Because the solicitors and directors of the Grand Trunk have made this error, the people of Canada, who are the vendees and purchasers of the road, are asked to step in and confirm and make legal the blunder that the Grand Trunk representatives themselves have made. It seems to me that the minister is going just a little too far when he asks this Parliament solemnly and seriously to say we are so anxious to take over this railway, that we have made such a splendid bargain that we are prepared to say: It does not matter about your mistake, we are going to ratify the agreement to save any further trouble. It does appear to me that this is absolutely irregular and opposed to all principles of business dealing between a vendor and a vendee. That is the first consideration.
The next point I want to take up with my hon. friend is the fact that these eight or twelve stockholders were not notified of this meeting. If they were not notified of the meeting they had no right to go to the meeting and to state any objection or consider the question in so far as they were concerned. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this Parliament should at least be the guardian of the minority of the stockholders and see to it that this bargain is not
put into effect until the Grand Trunk Company give every one of their stockholders an opportunity of being heard when the question is being discussed at the meeting. Under these circumstances it seems to me that the minister is going a little bit too far in coming to this House and asking it to ratify this agreement without giving any further or more detailed information in regard to the condition of the railway and what it is going to mean to this country. It is an unusual request that the minister makes and one to which this House should give very serious consideration.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Just as you took the Chair, Mr. Chairman, I made a very reasonable request to the minister for information in the full confidence that if he had the information he would give it to the committee. One point was as to the physical condition of the road. With regard to his information he is not any farther advanced than he was last year. He had the famous letter from Mr. Kelley, the manager of the road. He had that letter then; he has that letter now; nothing more, nothing less. I submit to this committee and to the Canadian people that in dealing with so vast a proposition as to taking over of the whole property of this company we should scarcely be satisfied as to the physical condition and value of the road upon the mere evidence of a letter of the manager of the road. It would be his duty, no matter how conscientious he was otherwise, in the interest of the shareholders, to make the best possible showing for the road. I heard the letter read last year; there is very little to it. It is hardly conceivable that the minister and the Government should ask this country to ratify that agreement when we have no evidence of the physical condition of the road except that which is afforded by a single letter of the manager of the Grand Trunk railway. The minister says that as far as the physical condition of the road is concerned he believes it is first class. We have a report on the physical condition signed by at least two men some time in the year 1916- a commission appointed by this Government for the purpose of ascertaining the physical condition not only of the Grand Trunk but of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern. One of the commissioners was the present Finance Minister in this Government (Sir Henry Drayton) who must furnish the money for the purchase of this road. That hon. gentleman reported in 1916 that the road was in bad shape, and that it

subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has stated that the Drayton-Acworth report disclosed the fact that the Grand Trunk railway at that time was not in good physical condition, and that $50,(Du,000 would be required to bring it up to proper standard, and he has asked me how much money has been expended on the road since that report was made. He could hardly expect us to have that information, for the reason that we would have no right to examine the books of the Grand Trunk in order to ascertain how much money had been expended upon the line since the submission of the Drayton-Acworth report. That information cannot be obtained until an investigation has been made. Such an investigation is to be undertaken, and in addition the arbitrators will be required to examine into the physical condition of the road-in fact they must look into the whole condition of the railway and make their award accordingly. As to how much money it will take to bring the Grand Trunk up to the condition suggested by my hon. friend, I can only repeat that the Grand Trunk officials themselves, as well as the officers of the Canadian National system, are of opinion that the Grand Trunk is in as good a state as other Canadian railways, but that as a result of war conditions it will have to be improved. That is a question of maintenance, and the work of improvement will be undertaken in the same way that other roads are carrying out improvements.
The hon. gentleman based his argument on the Drayton-Acworth report, but I think he will bear me out in the statement that the same commission strongly recommended that the Grand Trunk be taken over and joined up with the Canadian Northern system. In other words, they declared it would be impossible for the Grand Trunk railway to continue solvent if it were left by itself and compelled to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific as a part of its system. The same commission recommended that we should guarantee the debenture stocks and pay something by way of dividends on the first, second and third preference stocks. If the hon. gentleman will carefully read the report in question and compare it with the Bill that was passed at the last session of Parliament, he will see that in the terms agreed upon for taking over the Grand Trunk and its subsidiary companies, the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth Cofnmission are being carried out.
It has been explained so many times I almost hesitate to take up time by repeating it, that as regards taking over the Grand

Trunk Railway system we are in this position:	Owing to the Grand Trunk Pacific
being in the condition in which it is, if we did not take over the Grand Trunk, the parent company, the latter would have to go into insolvency. Rightly or wrongly, Parliament last session decided that it was not in the public interest to permit the Grand Trunk to go into insolvency, but that the Government should take over the Grand Trunk and its subsidiary companies, including the Grand Trunk Pacific, and make these lines part of the National Railway system of Canada. That having been decided upon, the necessary agreement was drawn and has been before -the House for some time. The suggestion of the leader of the Opposition that we should simply content ourselves with rectifying the two mistakes that were made, means that there would have to be another meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders to ratify these corrections.
I know what the hon. member would say in reply to that: "We are willing, in addition, to ratify this agreement in so far as the two companies are concerned." Of course, I think he means tha^But let me state further, and it has been brought to the attention of the House, that a question was raised by the solicitors in England for the Government as to' notice having been properly [DOT] given to the eight shareholders in Canada. There is no question about notice having been duly given to the 70,000 shareholders in England. The question was raised although it -was admitted that six ol those eight shareholders were in England and had received notice there. That question having been submitted to the Deputy Minister of Justice and our solicitor, it was thought advisable to have the agreement confirmed by Parliament so that no possible question as to its validity could be raised in future. The only persons who can be affected by the ratification are those two shareholders in Canada. At the present time they hold a very small amount of the four per cent stock guaranteed by the- Grand Trunk Railwray, and they will be affected to the extent that that same stock will be guaranteed by the Dominion Government instead of by the Grand Trunk Railway, so that they will be in a much better position. I may add that the Grand Trunk solicitors in England take the position that this stock is non-voting debenture stock, and that even if those two stockholders had received notice they would not have a right to vote.
When the Minister of Justice explained the position last week he stated that this
question having been raised it is thought better that Parliament and the people should feel that when the agreement is finally acted upon there remain no question of doubt as to its legality. Of course,, the hon. member is against the agreement as a whole, he does not favour the taking over of the Grand Trunk, and he expressed that opinion last year also. No one can object to his entertaining that opinion, but I feel that when a majority of this House passes on any question it is finally settled, and it is for the honour of Parliament and of the country that the agreement should be carried out.
Mr. JAiOOBS: I would like to have some information from the minister as to whether he is aware that last year the Grand Trunk line between Montreal and Toronto was in such an unsafe condition that the Board ot Railway Commissioners ordered the company to make the repairs necessary to insure the safety of the travelling public?

speechtext:
I think I know that
part of the line as well as the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National lines between Montreal and Toronto, for I travel over them frequently, and I must frankly say that my impression is that the Grand Trunk line is in better condition than either of the other two railways, and I think that is the impression of the public as well. I have not heard of any complaints. I do know that last year the company did a great deal of work between Montreal and Toronto, and they are still doing a great deal of work in the way of improving the line, for the reason that during the war they were up against it in getting rails and ties just the same as were all other railway companies. I live close to the Grand Trunk tracks and I travel over them every week, and for a year at least since the war the company have had new ties all along the line. I would not be a bit surprised at a report being made that probably some portion of the line was not in as good condition as it should be, but the same thing applies to the other railways, for the reports I have received are to the effect that the other railways are npt in very good condition. I think the hon. member will agree with me that the same condition exists in the United States, the whole transportation system of that country having been allowed to run down on account of the inability during the war to get rails, ties, and labour to make current repairs.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman a few' minutes ago made the remark that he was

anxious to see this agreement carry so as to effect a saving by getting the roads under one management and having more uniformity in operation. I am rather skeptical on that subject. Two years ago we passed a law incorporating the Canadian National Railway Company for that very same purpose, but the company has not yet been organized, and none of the promises which were made at the time as to economy, uniformity and better service to the public has been kept'. Here we are to-day with the Canadian National Railway Company unorganized-supposed to be operating, and not operating. The Order in Council authorized under that Act has not yet been passed. I have asked time and again for a return to get the Order in Council, but I am always sent the Order in Council that was passed previous to the incorporation of the Canadian National Railway Company. Is it any wonder that I am rather skeptical about promises made in this House to induce us to pass such agreements? The present conditions work an injustice to the public. The Canadian National Railway Company may be operating more than the Canadian Northern Railway, but not by virtue of the Act which two years ago we passed under closure because the Government were in such a hurry, but which has not yet been utilized. Before I proceed let me put one question to the minister:	Is
the Canadian National Railway Company now organized; and, if so, who are the directors, and when were they appointed?
Mr. .T. D. REID: At the time that Act was being passed I explained that we required it for the purpose of transferring to one company the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental railways and any other railways which we might take over by purchase or lease. I stated also that we expected to take over the Grand Trunk Railway system; at a ty rate, I think I did mention it. All the railways owned and controlled by the Government to-day are being operated in this way.

That is all right; we may differ on the subject of gargoyles as well as on the subject of the administration of railways. My grievance is that this Act to incorporate the Canadian National Railway Company was passed two years ago under false pretenses. That is a serious
9	p.m. charge, but I make it coldly and deliberately. I think before I speak, and I say exactly what I think. That Act was passed ostensibly for the purpose of bringing all these railways under one administration. We discussed the expropriation clause of that Act; it was the subject of quite a debate. I contended at the time that the expropriation clause was unfair; that if the Government wanted to go into the railway business they should take their chances the same as any other railway company. But they have not done it. Now, if I * desire to bring an fttion against the Transcontinental railway I have to write to the Secretary of State; he turns the matter over to the Minister of Justice; the Minister of Railways gets it; then it is sent to Mr. Hanna in Toronto; and subsequently it reaches the superintendent of the line.

speechtext: Why, it has already taken seven months to reach a certain stage in connection with a small claim made by a lumberman whose bush was burned last year through the negligence of employees of that Government road. So it is with the Intercolonial. The main object of passing that Act two years ago was not to ratify an Order in Council that had previously been passed. I asked my hon. friend whether that Order in Council that he referred to had been passed prior or subsequent to the Act of two years ago, and he has to admit that the Order in Council came first. As I say, that Act was passed, not to ratify an Order in Council, but to better conditions then existing. But, although that Act has been on the statute book for some time nothing has been done to carry out its terms. For my part, I shall not accept as an excuse the argument that the Grand Trunk was not then a part of the system and that the Government intended to take it over. My hon. friend may turn aside to discuss gargoyles or anything else that he likes, but I want to get at the facts. The member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) this afternoon gave us an answer to the question: If you are going to increase your business, how are you going to carry it on? The Government are bound, in view of the promises which they have made to the people, to put the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern under the same administration, not merely, by virtue of an Order in Council, but with due regard to legal conditions and legal considerations. I do not see why I should have to take out a petition of right in order that I may sue the Transcontinental whereas in the case of the Canadian Northern I can go before the courts of a province and get justice. Therefore, I am not ready to accept the reasons given by the minister-well, I shall not call them reasons; his explanation was merely a simulacre, as we would call it in French. He now asks us to ratify this agreement. It was provided when the agreement was made that Mr. Stockholder of the Grand Trunk should have the privilege of ratifying it, but that the people of Canada, who were paying for the road, should not. If blunders have been made, they will have to be rectified. But this agreement was brought before the House during a session that had been called for quite another purpose, and the people had no time to examine it. Before we give our assent to this ratification, every bit of information pertaining to this matter, so far as hon. members desire it, should be brought down.

Having learnt some philosophy at college, whenever I was placed in this unfortunate position of choosing between the President of the Privy Council and the murderous Lenine and the treacherous Trotsky, I would say to myself "De deux maux il faut choisir le moindre." The President of the Privy Council forgot- when he was talking to us about Bolshevism and its dangers, that he was one of the leading Bolsheviks in this country, because he promoted the general nationalization of public utilities- What is the Soviet system? What are the "commissaires" in Russia? I do not wish to make a comparison that will hurt the feelings of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways., but he is .a "oommissaire".
A commissaire is a gentleman who takes over all the industries of a country and runs them in the name, and on behalf, of the government of that country. Some people have been entrusted with the Tunning of mills; others have been given the control of railways, and to others,-and this is a very pleasant task,-has been given the guidance of young ladies and old maidens in the direction of matrimony.
So it is that I say that this Government

is introducing Bolshevism. We may have defects in our province, Mr. Chairman, but there are certain things we hold sacred; they are our traditions, our religion, and our households. I say that the time has come for the representatives of the people of Canada to put a stop to this radical policy of the present Government, especially when Bolshevism is introduced into this country by a minister who carries a Bible in one hand and a temperance tract in the other. Let people be shown in their true colours. If the hon. President of the Privy Council is a Bolshevist, let him not put on the mask of a Methodist in this House. In discussing this question in the light of past events, I say that after the declarations heard on the other side as to >
nationalization, this Government is placing the country in danger of very soon having a soviet government.
I know the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is surprised. He would not like to belong to a soviet government. A good Irishman is he when in Canada. Some people say he is not as good when he reaches Paris and has to discuss the Irish situation facing Lloyd George.

subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Taxes on what, Mr. Chairman? It is very easy for hon. members to get up and declare generally that we have got to impose taxes. But we should know what kind of taxes they wish to impose. The farmers have started a new movement. Their movement may be good or it may be bad, but it will only lead somewhere if they have a definite programme. It is very easy to talk of meeting deficits with taxes, but I would like the members of the new party, or the members opposite to tell us what taxes they would impose.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as I said, the railway situation in Canada is so bad that every business man in the country is opposed to the present policy of the Government. Nevertheless, in accordance with advice given by a former member of the Cabinet they "carry on." I think they will carry on till they are carried out, and the sooner the better.
Mr. MoQREA: I have been listening with a good deal of attention to this debate ever since its inception. I have heard the explanation given by the Minister of Railways and by hon. gentlemen supporting the Government, and I have come to the conclusion that the Government are wandering and are lost with respect to the simplest and most common-sense business principles in connection with this railway system of theirs. We have been for years operating the Intercolonial railway as a government-owned road. We have also been operating the Canadian Northern for some considerable time, and yet the Government do not seem to have made up their minds with respect to the simplest pair of the policy involved, and that is the question of rates. The Minister of Railways has not yet announced what is going to be the Government's programme. On a former occasion I said, and it is scarcely necessary to repeat the statement,

that I am opposed to government ownership of railways, or anything else of that character, first, last and all the time. 1 am convinced, after the experience of a lifetime in business, that the Government cannot carry on an undertaking of that nature either economically or intelligently. Why? For the simple reason-and you will find it to be the case if you examine the situation closely-that while there are some good men occasionally in the employ of the Government the great majority of them are men who have failed at everything else and cannot make a living in any other way than by applying to the Government for positions and jobs. I would like to ask any hon. gentleman in this House, or outside of it, who has had any business experience, if he thinks he can profitably or economically conduct and manage a business with men of that class. Now, to my mind-and when I say this I feel that I am in exactly the same position as the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt); I am speaking possibly against my own personal interests-there is ho reason why the Government should not allow railway rates to be increased proportionately with the cost of operating those railways before the war. Within the last five or six years the cost of wages, of equipment, of material-the cost of everything in connection with the operation of a railway or any other industry-has at least doubled. That being the case what increase has taken place in railway rates? Those rates have been increased forty per cent. When the railway companies asked for a further increase in rates from the Board of Railway Commissioners that board-I presume taking thei*-advice from the Government-simply told them, "No, you cannot have any increase in rates." Now is it reasonable, or in accordance with the dictates of common sense to ask the railway companies that are giving this country service to carry on the freight and passenger traffic on an increase in rates of simply forty per cent when the cost to-day of operating their systems is at least one hundred per cent higher than it was five years ago? It surely is not. Yet the Government do not seem to have any policy on this question. When the Minister of Railways is asked what is going to be the policy of the Government he replies, "I cannot tell, the people will have to decide that." I think it is about time the Government reached a decision on this question. If this railway system is going to be operated under government manage-
ment it is time for the Government to adopt the simplest common-sense and business principles. We have been told that the reason why they do not increase the rates on the Government railways is because if they did so, the Canadian Pacific would participate in that increase, and that would be a crime. If the Canadian Pacific railway had been managed as the Canadian Northern railway and practically every other railway in this; country has been managed it would be in the same position. It is because the Canadian Pacific railway has been well managed that the company has made a success of the undertaking. Evidently the: purpose of the Government is to penalize thrift and good management by saying to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company:	We will
not increase the -rates on the government-owned roads lest you should participate in the benefits. In my judgment that is neither good business nor honesty.
During the past few years when railway strikes have been threatened, the Minister of Labour has been requested to intervene and settle the difficulties between the railway companies and their employees. What has been the result? In every instance the minister has sided with the employees and has allowed them an advance in wages. I am not complaining of that. The cost of living is so high to-day that I do not think the men are getting more than enough to live on. But what'about the railway that is giving this country good service on a forty per cent increase in rates, whereas the cost of equipment and labour has at least doubled? I think the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) yesterday advocated keeping down the freight rates to their present level. My theory is that there should be a limit to the amount of increase to be granted, but if the cost of operation has increased one hundred per cent and the increase cannot be avoided is there any reason why freight rates should not be increased in proportion? If this government-owned railway system after getting such increase showed a deficit, let the country bear that deficit; but until the system is allowed to charge rates in proportion to the cost of operation it is not . fair to the country as a whole that the _ people who use the roads-and I am one of them-should not pay rates in proportion to the increased operating cost
The Minister of Railways informed the House last week that the roads under government control and operation show for the past year a deficit of $47,000,000. And that

is the loss on operation only; so far as I understand no allowance is made for depreciation of rolling stock and plant. I think that if to that 847,000,000 loss we add a fair amount for depreciation and wear and tear of rolling stock, and on top of that again add a fair rate of interest on the capital invested, we shall find the deficit is probably nearly twice $47,000,000. Therefore I think it is well to advise the Government to adopt some honest method of book-keeping so that the country may be informed of the actual deficit which will have to be provided for out of the public funds. When discussing the Grand Trunk Bill last year we were told by the minister and by other members of the Government that one of the reasons for taking over the Grand Trunk system was to secure the advantage of its Portland terminals. We were also told that the National Railway system was going to be placed in the hands of a commission entirely independent of all governmental interference. Some ten days ago we were discussing how export freight originating on the Grand Trunk and the Government Railway system would be routed, and the Minister of Railways said that he was going to see to it that all such freight would be routed by Canadian ports -Montreal, Quebec, St. John, and Halifax. Those two statements are contradictory and require explanation. If he intends to route export traffic by Canadian ports I want to know, why is it so necessary to acquire the Grand Trunk railway especially to .secure the advantage of its Portland terminals? That was held out as one of the reasons why we must absorb the Grand Trunk and round out our National Railway system. Then I want to know, by what authority does the Minister of Railways tell the people of this country that he is going to see to it that all traffic will be routed in a particular way? If I understood his statement a year ago, he was to have nothing to say about the management of our National Railway system-but it was to be under the supreme control of a commission entirely dependent of political interference.
I do not wish to take up any more time. I merely desire to impress upon the Government-and I do not speak from any disposition to be unduly critical-that the question of how to fix rates ought to be so simple that there should not be any hesitation in dealing with it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. CO-PP: Was the deficit under government operation in the United States greater than under private operation?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I take it that it was; I cannot give my hon. friend the figures as to private operation. As all hon. members know, during the war the United States Government administered all the railroads of that country, and owing to the most remarkable McAdoo award, wages were increased enormously,, and the same rate of increase was applied in Canada. I shall not reiterate what I said last night about these roads that have fallen into the hands of the Government. I quite see how hon. gentlemen may criticise, and probably they criticise with justice. But as was stated so frequently in this House during the last two sessions, the question is, what alternative would you suggest? The operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific ceased; they threw up their hands. The Canadian Northern was at the end of its tether, and the Government had either to take it over or continue to pay out tens of millions by way of subsidies to keep it in operation. So with the Transcontinental. In my judgment it would be in the interests of the 10 p.m. country to abandon that road for ten or twenty years, because if you are going to charge higher freight rates to make up enormous deficits on capital, the road will not begin to pay running expenses. Where, then, are we going to get to? Then the old Grand Trunk came to the end of its tether, and the Government, which, after all, represents the people, was obliged to take it over. No hon. member has not been able to suggest any alternative to That-course during the last two or three sessions. So we have an enormous system, not voluntarily owned by the people,, but forced upon the people.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Why not let the Canadian Pacific take the Grand Trunk?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Well, that might be; I do not knowr that the Canadian Pacific wants the Grand Trunk. But we have to look at -this thing on its merits-or demerits. Unless a decent alternative can be offered which will appeal to the common sense of members and to those who have the interests of the country at heart, why denounce such public ownership as we have? There is no alternative; there is nothing else to do. We have to carry the load; but -let us not place a vast additional burden upon the country in the way of high freight rates three-quarters of w'hich would be
fMr. Richardson. 1
placed upon us for the benefit of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company which does not- need increased rates. I do not want to be understood as being opposed to the Canadian Pacific railway. I have watched that railway develop from its infancy, I was in the Press Gallery when the charter was granted thirty-five years ago-and I pay tribute to its splendid management and to the ability of the men who have been in charge of it. We, the people of this country, have this problem to wrestle with. There is no alternative; so let us make the best of a bad bargain, let us do the best we can w'ith our nationally-owned system.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the Government to increase freight rates in order to meet the deficit on operation, which appears to be very large?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I explained last night the position so far as that is concerned. The question of railway rates is entirely in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners, from whose decision there is a right of appeal to the Governor in Council. In the case of appeal to the Governor in Council, his decision shalll be final. There would be only one way to prevent the railways from getting an increase and that would be to pass a Bill establishing the present rates as maximum rates. The management claim that the rates should be increased and unless the Government should urge them not to take part in these proceedings, they will doubtless continue to urge an increase. The hon. member can, therefore, see our position in the matter.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
We are not certain, then, whether there will be an increase or not. I wish to put myself on record as strongly opposed to an increase of freight rates on the Government railways. I do not know what the merchant or dealer in other parts of Canada does, but in my part of the country when freight rates are increased, the consumer, the poor man generally, pays the difference. I am speaking not of the rich man, but of the poor man generally. Whenever an increase of fifty cents is made in the rate on a barrel of flour, the poor man has to pay that fifty cents, because the merchant does not lose a cent, he simply imposes the tax on his goods. That is the reason why I am strongly against the increase. I might refer to the matter of income taxes, although that is a subject not quite in order in this discussion, and state that merchants throughout the country, men worth probably half a million or

more, are being taxed heavily. Do these merchants pay the tax? Yes, but they impose the tax on their goods, and I and other poor men like me have to pay it. In that way, the whole burden from beginning to end has to be borne by the consumer. We should not impose any further burden on them, and I would ask the Government to curtail the expenses of the railways in order that the revenue may cover the expenses; otherwise I think it would be better to throw the railways away or to give them to somebody else.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have no desire to prolong the debate in committee unduly, nor have I any particular desire to sound a discordant note in the remarks that have been made from this side of the House. At the same time, the criticism of nationalization of railways which has been made from this side and the lack of support from the other side of that principle have been to me somewhat of a disappointment. Last year, when the Government was led by the then Acting Prime Minister, who was also Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), we had a pronouncement that the Government had now become the champion of public ownership, and members on the opposite side supported the Acting Prime Minister in that statement, I am surprised and, as I say, disappointed, to find that there is nothing of that kind in the discussion that is now taking place. At that time I expressed myself as being in favour of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, and I have not changed my opinion. I still believe that the Grand Trunk ought to become part of the National Railway system. I fear this -and I said so last year-that we are going to pay probably $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 more for the Grand Trunk than we ought to pay, and I was of the opinion then, and I am still, that this House should finally pass upon the award which the arbitrators will make.
Last year, the then Acting Prime Minister stated that a former Government had left, in his homely language, two dirty babies on the Government's doorstep, which were a heritage from a former Government. I am not going into the merits or demerits of that, but I will say that the Acting Prime Minister of last year himself deposited s'till another dirty baby on the doorstep of this country -the Grand Trunk railway. I suppose, therefore, we may say that we now have triplets: The Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk. For 96J
my part, I believe that the three belong together, and I believe that those who now quite honestly and sincerely oppose the acquisition of the Grand Trunk are, in effect, denying to that last baby the right and privilege of being properly cleaned up and brought up as a decent member of society. Indeed I hope and believe that in the end these babies may grow strong enough to assist in supporting the rest of the family. I believe that the railways of this country will in time be one of its greatest assets, and they will discharge a real service. We sometimes lose sight of the objects of public ownership. The primary object of public ownership is service to the people at cost or at as nearly cost as possible.
What I rose to speak chiefly about was this: That it is an entirely unfair statement to make that public ownership if a failure because of the fact that during the last year the government-owned railways showed a deficit of $47,000,000. I admit that a loss of $47,000,000 on the Government railways ought to be disquieting to every member of this House and is disquieting to the people o_f this country. It is not any more so, to my mind, than the fact that this country has to-day a gross debt of more than $3,000,000,000 and a net debt of a good deal more than $2,000,000,000. That great debt, like the-deficits in railway operations, is the result to some extent of things over which we have no control, and to some extent also of extravagance and mismanagement on the part of the Government with regard to the debt and, perhaps, on the part of those who control and manage these railways as regards those railways. But surely those members -and I include those on this side of the House-who have taken as proof of the failure of public ownership of railways this fact of a deficit of $47,000,000, do not think that is a fair statetment; they surely would not say that if those railways had remained under private ownership, they would have shown anything but a deficit. In 1918, if my memory serves me correctly, the Canadian Northern railway showed a loss of something like $14,000,000, and we know that because of circumstances, such as increases in the wage bill of the railway and other reasons, those losses have been increasing from year to year. I think it is even a fact that the earnings of the Canadian Pacific last year were somewhat less than they were the year before.
Nationalization, or public ownership of railways may be right or it may be wrong, but I want to make this point, that the

loss of $47,000,000 last year by the National railways is to itself not a proof of the failure of public ownership, because we would have had that loss anyway. We must recognize the fact that had the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific continued under private ownership, the losses would have resulted and the Government of Canada would have had to foot the bill just the same. We hear the Canadian Pacific quoted continually as a proof of the superiority of private ownership and operation of railways. What makes the- Canadian Pacific successful? Two things: They have an all-round railway fully equipped all along the line, and then they have good management, the first of course, being the result of the latter. If you have the same-thing with the National railways, you may expect a similar result. You must, therefore, organize the National roads into one complete road, and that is my reason for supporting the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway, because I contend that it is absolutely impossible to make the roads which we now own and control a financial success without the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. The latter supplies the necessary branches and terminals in Eastern Canada, which the National railways do not possess now.
Then there is the other consideration, that you must have good management. Last year I asked the Minister of Railways Whether it was his intention to change the management of the road. It is no particular pleasure to me, nor perhaps to other members of the committee, constantly ' to harp on and criticize the management of the National railways, but I do not believe that the people of this country have complete faith in the management, and I think that the Government should take some note of that state of the public mind. The minister at that time assured the House that an entire re-organization of the management of the National roads would be undertaken. So far as I know, nothing in that direction has yet been done. Perhaps the minister is postponing the re-organization until the Grand Trunk has been actually taken over by the Government, but unless this entire reorganization takes place I am sure that the cause of public ownership will receive a setback from which it is not likely to recover for a great many years.
Just a word on the question of rates. The Minister of Railways stated the other day that in order to make up the deficit we must either increase the rates or dip into the
fMr. Euler.]
public treasury. In discussing these alternatives he made the statement that one great objection to increasing the rates was the fact that it would put some $51),000,000 more into the coffers of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He seemed to think that was a fatal objection. I wonder if it has ever occurred to this public-ownership government that here is a ready remedy. It may be considered rank heresy for me to suggest this: If the Government took over the Canadian Pacific as well, a road that is a paying institution, they would not have to increase the rates so very much. The Canadian Pacific last year made $22,000,000 of profits, so we would not have to increase the rates so very much. We would not require an additional $50,000,000. If the Government took over the Canadian Pacific, a very slight increase in rates would probably put the system on a basis where it could pay expenses.

speechtext: I make no such suggestion. I do not believe in robbing anybody. If we took over the Canadian Pacific, I would expect the shareholders to be paid what the property was worth. What I am speaking of is profits.

The taking over of the Canadian Pacific has been suggested by The Globe.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I realize that it is an impracticable suggestion at the present time, because our commitments are very heavy, but the time will come when this country will own not only the" railways we now have and the Grand Trunk, but also the Canadian Pacific unless through wrong policies and bad management the cause of public ownership is so bedevilled as not to give the system a chance. So far as rates are concerned, I am thoroughly of opinion that the rates ought to be such that the raods will carry themselves. I do not think it is fair that some of the people of this country should be asked to pay for the railway service that is being given to other people in this country. Public ownership means service at cost, but it does not mean service at less than cost, and I want to put myself on record on this question of rates, that the only proper thing to do is to make the rates such that the neople who receive the service will pay for it.

Does my hon. friend mean that the Government should go on and in-

crease the rates and spend money even to the point of extravagance?

Extravagance is the very
thing I have been condemning. My whole point is this:	The man who is receiving
service, ought to pay for that service. Let every tub stand on its own bottom.

What does the minister
mean by saying that the Grand Trunk have changed their fiscal year? speechtext: I want no more quibbling. I want the minister to give me a straight answer to my question. The Grand Trunk year has not been changed. It ended on the 31st of December in 1918, and it ended on the 31st of December in 1919. I am asking whether the minister has in his department the statement of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the fiscal year ending December 31, 1919, and how the earnings for that year compare with the earnings for 1918.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

I am not quibbling at all. I quite understand the hon. gentleman's question, but my deputy minister tells me that we have not got the Grand Trunk official statement for the year 1919.
I think that is a fair answer. I was right in saying that the fiscal year of the railway companies ended on June 30, until the date was changed by Act of Parliament, to December 31. He does not know anything about what the operations were in 1919 as compared with 1918 and 1917. When he is asked by my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Air. AlcKenzie) to-night what amount of money was spent on the road, he says that he does not think that the department has that information. Any one can go to the library and get that information for 1915-16. The department has that information and it should be [DOT]willing to give it to this committee. I do not think there is any necessity for passing this legislation, it does not amount to anything, and the Government has not given us an explanation of why it brought the Bill in. But if the Government is determined to go ahead and conclude the bargain, it means nothing

at all. It has no information to give the House and no reason it is asking for the ratification of the agreement. The minister has no more information than he had a year ago, and the information (which he had then did not amount to anything. I think the minister ought to be able to tell us the earnings of the Grand Trunk for 1919. That information is in the department, and the committee is entitled to it. If he refuses to give the information we cannot do anything about it, but I will tell him this, that (when he comes to pass his Estimates he will have to furnish us with more information than he has given on this Bill if he has any expectation of getting them through.

speechtext:
I am not prepared to say that is wrong, but I think that quite a good argument could be put up on the other side. The House will note the language of that section of the agreement:
The Managing Committee may, with the consent of the Governor in Council-
Not with the consent of Parliament, but with the consent of the Governor in Council-
-borrow from the Government on Grand Trunk notes, or other obligations or securities approved of by the Governor in Council for the carrying on of the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system.
It might be contended with some fairness or force that when that clause is put into the agreement it contemplates borrowing and lending and that when the Government gives its sanction to that clause as a part of the agreement it clearly contemplates, by implication at all events, authority to lend. If there is any room for doubt at all it ought to be absolutely cleared up, and I was going to suggest, if the Minister of Justice had been in his place, that the addition of the following proviso would put it beyond question:
Nothing herein contained shall be constructed to permit any lending of money by the Government to the Managing Committee, mentioned in the fourth section of the said Agreement, without the specific authority of Parliament.
The minister may say that is what it means anyway, and if it is found ultimately to bear that meaning I shall be content with having put this view before the House.
I think I could argue with a good deal of force that if we accepted that .clause and put it in the agreement and it was ratified by Parliament it would contemplate not only the borrowing power but the lending

power. However, I do not want to repeat the argument, the Minister of Justice can read it in Hansard and if there is anything in it it can be dealt with at a later date.

speechtext: My hon. friend from Pont:ae (Mr. Cahill) in discussing this matter a few moments ago ashed the minister a question in regard to the operations, of the Grand Trunk Company for the year ending December, 1919. It is highly important, if we are to compare the operations of the railway for 1919 with those of 1918, that we should at least have some information on the subject, because it would mean very much to the committee and to the country. I trust the minister will not accuse me of attempting to argue from a wrong standpoint. I have no desire to insinuate in the least degree that he has the report in question; we have simply the word of my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) in regard to the matter. I do say this, however; The hon. gentleman on his responsibility stated that the information was in the department.

Now he may not know that it was in the department, but he must have the information that such a report has been prepared. If that report was prepared by the officials of the Grand Trunk it ought to be in the hands of the minister and he should submit it to this committee when he is asking for the passage of such an important Bill as this. If we had that report before us. and could compare the operations of the railway for the year 1919 with the operations of the year 1918, and see whether the comparison was a favourable or unfavourable one, it might have a very great deal of weight on the minds of hon. gentlemen as to whether it would be a proper thing to take over this road at the present time. The minister apparently comes to the conclusion that this is a trifling matter with which neither members of the House nor the people are concerned. I say to him that we on this side are eager and anxious, in the event of it being decided to carry out this arrangement that we should make a good bargain. If my hon. friend who spoke a few moments ago is correct in his statement that the operations of the Grand Trunk railway show that its acquisition would be beneficial to this country, that is all very well; but I do say that when we are considering a matter of such vast importance we are not exceeding our duties when we insist that my hon. friend who has charge of this Bill should bring whatever information is available before the House. Not only should private members have that information as a matter of courtesy from the minister, but the people of Canada should be given it as well so that they may understand that true condition of affairs and not find in acquiring this railway they were, to use a homely expression, " buying a pig in a poke ". Whatever information is required I insist, Mr. Chairman, should not have been drawn out of the minister, but should be given willingly, frankly and generously to this committe so that the matters as they come before us may be considered on the merits.

subtopic: BIDE TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I submit in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, that the Railway Department is playing unfairly with this Parliament and this committee. When we passed the Grand Trunk Acquisition Act last fall it was well understood that a board of arbitration was to be appointed to ascertain the value of this road. I am sure that the Minister of Justice and every business man in the House will agree with me that the Department of Railways should at once have set to work preparing the Government's case. But here we are on the 21st of April, and although it is said the arbitrators are about to be appointed, that department is not in possession of one scintilla of information in regard to the whole business.
The Government may treat us lightly on this side of the House, but I would ask hon. gentlemen who have to account to their constituents for their attitude on this very large question how they feel at the prospect of being called upon to ratify an agreement concerning which the Minister of Railways himself knows nothing at all, but which he asks them to vote for with their eyes shut. I cannot understand any minister, particularly an experienced minister like the Minister of Railways, knowing at least for the past month or two that he had to come before Parliament to ask for the ratification of this agreement, sitting down contentedly without giving any thought to securing the slightest information for the use of this House. The hon. minister will not say that he asked the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for their financial statement of last year and that they refused to furnish it to him. I venture to say that he has not asked for a single statement, but has simply taken the position that nothing was sent to his office. It was the duty of the minister to secure all the information he possibly could in order to be in a position to satisfy the House. But it looks as if he had made up his mind that no matter how barren he was of information, it was a foregone conclusion that hon. gentlemen supporting the Government would vote to pass this Bill. No clearer evidence of this attitude could be found than the position he finds himself in to-night.
At the opening of the discussion while the Speaker was in the Chair, and before the motion for second reading was passed, I made some statements in regard to the powers which I thought we had in respect to this agreement. Now that the Minister of Justice is in his plaice I feel more comfortable in making some observations in regard to the attitude we should take on this ratification. I wish particularly to call his attention to the fifteenth article of the agreement itself, where the limitations of this Parliament are acknowledged. It reads as follows:
Upon the preference and common stock being vested in the Government, or its nominees the Grand Trunk shall cause its board of directors and the board of directors of each company comprised in the Grand Tunk system, to resign or vacate their offices, as directors, at such time or times and in such manner as may be requested by the Government, and nominees of the Government shall be duly appointed to the vacancies caused thereby. Should any director of the Grand Trunk, or of any company comprised in the Grand Trunk system, which is within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, neglect -to resign or vacate his office in accordance with such request, the Governor in Council may declare the office of any such director to be vacant, on and after a date to be named in such order, and may appoint a director in his stead.
Two points in this article should be noticed. One is the provision for political appointees to every position that will be rendered vacant by the decree of the Government. We were told repeatedly that this road, as well as any other road controlled by the Government, was to be absolutely non-political in its management, but here we find that on a certain date every manager, official, and director of the Grand Trunk shall resign and their positions shall be filled by nominees of the Government. If I understand anything at all, it is that political friends entitled to consideration at the hands of the Government will be appointed to those positions, in utter disregard of the independent board of management which we were promised.
When I spoke on this point before I contended that we had no authority to deal with any matter beyond the territorial jurisdiction of this Parliament, and I think that is recognized by this article fifteen, which says that we shall deal with such and such matters as far as they are within the legislative authority of this Parliament. If that passage does not mean that we have no authority over certain things in connection with this business, then I cannot understand the true sense of those words. I start out then by saying that our limitations as a parliament are recognized by that para-
